title: Fluctuation force induced by quenched random polarizations
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Invited contribution to JCP's Special Topic on "Statistical Physics: From Quantum Fluctuations to Soft Matter and Viral Assemblies" honoring the memory of Rudolf Podgornik
summary: We investigate the zero-temperature behavior of the fluctuation force induced by random electric dipoles that are frozen into a material and incapable of fluctuating thermally. Examples of such materials are relaxor ferroelectrics. In terms of the setup and geometry, we focus on a layered system comprising two coplanar semi-infinite slabs separated by a distance $\ell$ as well as a system comprising a neutral atom in the vacuum located at a distance $\ell$ above the surface of a semi-infinite slab. For both systems, we consider the cases where the quenched random dipolar disorder occurs inside the bulk as well as on the surface of the slabs. In all of these cases, we find that the bulk (surface) dipolar disorder-induced fluctuation force grows with the mean square quenched electric dipole moment per unit volume (area). The bulk (surface) dipolar disorder-induced fluctuation pressure between two semi-infinite single-layered slabs decays with $\ell^{-3}$ ($\ell^{-4}$), whereas the bulk (surface) dipolar disorder-induced fluctuation force on an atom in the vacuum near a slab containing the disorder decays with $\ell^{-4}$ ($\ell^{-5}$). We also find that the quenched dipolar disorder-induced fluctuation force between two coplanar slabs can be repulsive and serve to enhance the ``nanolevitation effect" in a three-layered dielectric system that obeys the Dzyaloshinskii-Lifshitz-Pitaevskii condition.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the zero-temperature fluctuation force induced by quenched (frozen) random electric dipoles in materials like relaxor ferroelectrics. It studies two systems: two coplanar semi-infinite slabs separated by distance ℓ, and a neutral atom at distance ℓ above a slab. The force decays as power laws (ℓ⁻³ to ℓ⁻⁵ depending on bulk/surface disorder and geometry), and can be repulsive, enhancing the nanolevitation effect under the Dzyaloshinskii-Lifshitz-Pitaevskii condition.
AI.motivation: To understand the fluctuation forces arising from quenched (non-thermal) random electric dipoles, which differ from standard Casimir or thermal fluctuation forces, and to explore their potential role in repulsive forces and nanolevitation.
AI.method: Analytical theory of zero-temperature fluctuation forces induced by quenched random dipolar disorder, considering both bulk and surface disorder, in two geometries: (1) two coplanar semi-infinite slabs, and (2) a neutral atom above a semi-infinite slab.
AI.result: Bulk (surface) disorder-induced fluctuation pressure between two slabs decays as ℓ⁻³ (ℓ⁻⁴). Force on an atom near a slab decays as ℓ⁻⁴ (ℓ⁻⁵). The force can be repulsive and enhance nanolevitation in a three-layered dielectric system satisfying the Dzyaloshinskii-Lifshitz-Pitaevskii condition.
AI.conclusion: Quenched random dipolar disorder generates measurable fluctuation forces at zero temperature with distinct power-law scalings dependent on the dimensionality of the disorder (bulk vs. surface) and geometry, and these forces can be repulsive, offering a mechanism to enhance nanolevitation.

title: High-dimensional theory of the glass transition revisited: hopping and local defects
summary: The replicated liquid theory provides a microscopic mean-field description of the glass transition by combining the density functional theory of liquids with the replica method originally developed for spin glasses. In the conventional replica liquid theory, a glassy state is described by assuming that particles in different replicas undergo vibrational motion around common centers of mass, thereby forming molecules that contain one particle from every replica. Here we revisit this assumption by allowing each molecule to contain only a subset of replicas. This generalized formulation describes particle-level replica mismatches, which may be associated with non-vibrational motions such as particle hopping. We apply the theory to high-dimensional hard and harmonic spheres, where the mean-field description is expected to become exact. For hard spheres, replica mismatches destabilize the glassy metastable state and shift the dynamical transition to a significantly higher packing fraction, while leaving the leading thermodynamic glass transition unchanged. The resulting transition density agrees, at leading order in high dimensions, with the recent rigorous lower bound for random sphere packings obtained by Campos, Jenssen, Michelen, and Sahasrabudhe by using a discretized version of greedy Random Sequential Absorption, suggesting an algorithmic interpretation of the transition: grandcanonical dynamics is more efficient in high dimensional spaces than canonical one. For harmonic spheres at finite temperature, the glassy state contains a finite replica-mismatch fraction even at the thermodynamic ideal-glass transition, thereby shifting the transition point from that predicted by the conventional replica ansatz.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes replicated liquid theory by allowing replica mismatches (molecules containing subsets of replicas), finding that for high-dimensional hard spheres this destabilizes the glassy state and shifts the dynamical transition to match a rigorous lower bound from greedy RSA, while for harmonic spheres it shifts the ideal glass transition itself.
AI.motivation: The conventional replica liquid theory assumes particles in different replicas vibrate around common centers of mass (full-replica molecules). The authors revisit this assumption to describe particle-level replica mismatches that may capture non-vibrational motions like particle hopping, which are not accounted for in the standard ansatz.
AI.method: The authors generalize replica liquid theory by allowing each molecule to contain only a subset of replicas, then apply the formulation to high-dimensional hard spheres and harmonic spheres (where mean-field theory is exact). They analyze how replica mismatches affect the dynamical and thermodynamic glass transitions.
AI.result: For hard spheres, replica mismatches destabilize the glassy metastable state, shifting the dynamical transition to a higher packing fraction without changing the thermodynamic transition. The new transition density matches a rigorous lower bound from Campos et al. using greedy RSA. For harmonic spheres, replica mismatches persist even at the thermodynamic ideal-glass transition, shifting the transition point.
AI.conclusion: Replica mismatches are essential for a complete mean-field description of glasses. The agreement with the greedy RSA bound suggests an algorithmic interpretation: grandcanonical dynamics is more efficient than canonical dynamics in high dimensions.

title: On the robustness of noisy solutions in non-convex neural networks
summary: Optimization in non-convex neural network models is strongly influenced by the geometry of the solution space: sparse, isolated, point-like clusters are typically algorithmically inaccessible, whereas wide and flat regions can be found efficiently despite being relatively rare. At zero temperature this picture has been formalized in binary perceptrons through the overlap gap property (OGP), which limits algorithmic access to configurations with zero training error above a critical constraint density $α_{\rm OGP}$. Here we extend this description to finite temperature, where a positive training error is allowed and statistically penalized. We first show that the frozen one-step replica-symmetry-breaking solution, dominating the zero temperature equilibrium measure, survives at any finite temperature. We furthermore derive a general criterion, based on the smoothness of the single-pattern Gibbs weight near the decision boundary, that determines when a finite-temperature relaxation of the loss removes freezing. We then extend the OGP construction to finite temperature and show that dense, algorithmically accessible regions of finite-energy configurations persist beyond $α_{\rm OGP}$, up to a threshold $α_{\rm OGP}(ε)$ that grows with the allowed training error $ε$. Finally, in the teacher-student setting, we show that these wide, finite-energy regions still retain good generalization. Using a finite energy message-passing algorithm, we demonstrate numerically that thermal noise enables effective generalization in the regime of constraint densities where both recovering the teacher and finding a zero temperature solution are computationally hard.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the overlap gap property (OGP) analysis from zero-temperature to finite-temperature regimes in binary perceptrons, showing that thermal noise allows algorithmic access to dense regions of finite-energy solutions beyond the zero-temperature OGP threshold, enabling effective generalization even when zero-temperature solutions are computationally hard.
AI.motivation: To understand how finite temperature (allowing positive training error) affects the geometric landscape of non-convex neural network optimization, particularly to determine whether thermal relaxation can overcome the algorithmic barriers imposed by the overlap gap property at zero temperature.
AI.method: The authors extend the OGP framework to finite temperature by: (1) showing the frozen one-step replica-symmetry-breaking solution survives at finite temperature, (2) deriving a general criterion based on single-pattern Gibbs weight smoothness near the decision boundary to determine when finite-temperature relaxation removes freezing, (3) constructing a finite-temperature OGP threshold α_OGP(ε) that grows with allowed training error ε, and (4) using a finite-energy message-passing algorithm for numerical validation in the teacher-student setting.
AI.result: Dense, algorithmically accessible finite-energy regions persist beyond the zero-temperature OGP threshold up to a higher threshold α_OGP(ε) that increases with permitted training error. Finite-temperature relaxation can remove freezing when the Gibbs weight is smooth near the decision boundary. Thermal noise enables effective generalization in computationally hard regimes.
AI.conclusion: Thermal noise and finite-energy configurations can circumvent computational hardness barriers in non-convex neural network optimization, enabling good generalization in regimes where zero-temperature solutions are both inaccessible and unable to recover the teacher.

title: Quantum mechanics on the line with two origins
summary:
We study scalar and spinorial quantum dynamics on the standard line with two origins, \[
  \Ltwo=(\R_1\sqcup\R_2)/\!\sim,
  \qquad
  (x,1)\sim(x,2)\quad\text{for }x\neq0, \] equipped with its identity-glued smooth structure and flat metric. We first show that the ordinary scalar theory is insensitive to the doubled origin: every continuous map from \(\Ltwo\) to a Hausdorff space factors through the quotient \(q:\Ltwo\to\R\), while, for the natural measure, \[
  C^\infty(\Ltwo)\cong C^\infty(\R),
  \qquad
  L^2(\Ltwo)\cong L^2(\R). \] Accordingly, the natural scalar free Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent to the free Laplacian on \(\R\).
  The doubled origin remains visible, however, in the spinor line associated with the nontrivial spin structure. The oriented flat structure on \(\Ltwo\) admits two spin structures, distinguished by the relative transition sign on the two connected components of the chart overlap. For the nontrivial structure, these signs are opposite. This forces every continuous global spinor section to vanish at both origins and every smooth section to vanish there to infinite order. The associated first-order operator \[
  -i\,\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx} \] on compactly supported smooth twisted sections is symmetric but not essentially self-adjoint: its deficiency indices are \((1,1)\), and a self-adjoint first-order evolution requires an additional transmission condition at the origin. The natural positive quadratic form associated with the flat twisted structure instead yields the direct sum of two Dirichlet half-line Laplacians and hence perfect reflection. Thus the ordinary scalar theory does not detect the doubled origin, whereas the nontrivially glued spinor line does, although the spin structure alone does not determine a unique unitary transmission law.

AI.tldr: The paper studies quantum dynamics on a line with two origins (a non-Hausdorff manifold). Scalar fields are insensitive to the doubled origin—the theory reduces to that on ℝ. However, the nontrivial spin structure on this space forces spinors to vanish at both origins, leading to a first-order Dirac operator that is symmetric but not essentially self-adjoint (deficiency indices (1,1)). The natural quadratic form yields two decoupled Dirichlet half-line Laplacians, giving perfect reflection.
AI.motivation: To understand whether non-Hausdorff features in spacetime (e.g., the line with two origins) can be detected by quantum fields, and to contrast the behavior of scalar fields (which do not detect it) with spinor fields (which do).
AI.method: The paper considers the manifold L₂ = (ℝ₁ ⊔ ℝ₂)/∼ with identity-glued smooth structure and flat metric. It analyzes the scalar quantum theory (continuous maps, smooth functions, L² spaces, free Hamiltonian) and then spinor theories (spin structures, transition signs, twisted sections, first-order Dirac operator, deficiency indices, quadratic forms).
AI.result: (1) Scalar theory: C∞(L₂) ≅ C∞(ℝ) and L²(L₂) ≅ L²(ℝ); the free Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent to the free Laplacian on ℝ. (2) Nontrivial spin structure: global continuous spinors must vanish at both origins; smooth sections vanish to infinite order. The Dirac operator −i d/dx on compactly supported twisted sections is symmetric but not essentially self-adjoint with deficiency indices (1,1). The natural positive quadratic form gives the direct sum of two Dirichlet half-line Laplacians, implying perfect reflection.
AI.conclusion: The doubled origin is invisible to scalar fields but is detectable by the nontrivial spin structure. However, the spin structure alone does not uniquely determine the unitary transmission law; additional boundary conditions are needed.

title: Malleability of transformations on the ciphertext in noisy Quantum public key encryption
comment: Template (57 pages). summary: We characterize a noisy variant of a Quantum public encryption protocol recently introduced by Malavolta and Walter which demonstrated that the notion of everlasting security can be rigorously formulated for Quantum key distribution after two rounds of interaction between Alice and Bob. To address one possible direction of research that is related to injecting noise in the cryptographic protocol related to Quantum key distribution we formulate arguments for further examining the notion of everlasting security through malleability assumptions on transformations of the ciphertext. Assumptions surrounding malleability were introduced by Maurer and Tackmann for the purposes of comparing how authenticate then encrypt, and encrypt then authenticate, protocols behave through a variety of expressions for the forwarding error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities. Such probabilities are put to further use for obtaining connections between the indistinguishability and security threshold for a cryptographic protocol of interests. To further build upon such associations we demonstrate, through an adaptation of the Gentle Measurement Lemma from Quantum information theory, how upper bounds on the trace distance can be used to generalize the negligibility function obtained by Malavolta and Walter in the noiseless setting. Besides the fact that the negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold it continues to remain of interest to determine whether computations provided in this work for upper bounding the trace distance can be related to other settings that are centered more on game-theoretic approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes a noisy variant of a quantum public encryption protocol by Malavolta and Walter, using malleability assumptions and the Gentle Measurement Lemma to generalize the negligibility function from the noiseless setting, showing a higher security threshold in noisy environments, and exploring connections to game-theoretic approaches.
AI.motivation: To address the direction of injecting noise into quantum cryptographic protocols related to Quantum Key Distribution, and to further examine the notion of everlasting security through malleability assumptions on ciphertext transformations.
AI.method: The authors use malleability assumptions (from Maurer and Tackmann) to analyze forward error, deleting error, and reconstruction probabilities. They adapt the Gentle Measurement Lemma from quantum information theory to derive upper bounds on trace distance, which are used to generalize the negligibility function from Malavolta and Walter's noiseless setting to a noisy setting.
AI.result: The negligibility function in the noisy setting is related to a higher security threshold compared to the noiseless case. Upper bounds on trace distance are established, which can potentially be related to game-theoretic approaches.
AI.conclusion: The noisy variant of the quantum public encryption protocol exhibits a higher security threshold. The authors suggest further investigation into whether the trace distance upper bounds can be connected to game-theoretic settings.

title: Exact Finite-Dimensional Evaluation of Homodyne Quantum Trajectories for Single-Quadrature Hamiltonian
summary: Simulation of nonlinear stochastic master equations generally requires trajectory-level evolution of large Hilbert-space density matrices, making strongly nonlinear continuously monitored systems computationally challenging. Here we identify an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems consisting of polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, and homodyne measurement of the same quadrature. For Gaussian initial states, we derive an exact finite-dimensional stochastic representation of the conditional dynamics for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments $\langle Q^mP^n\rangle$ through closure of the conditional momentum hierarchy. The resulting coefficient equations depend only on the Hamiltonian degree and moment order, with computational complexity $\mathcal{O}(C_{d,n}T)$, independent of the Hilbert-space dimension. The method requires no Fock-space truncation, Gaussian approximation, or moment closure approximation. Numerical simulations demonstrate agreement with direct stochastic master equation evolution and establish an efficient exact method for studying nonlinear homodyne trajectories in this class of continuously monitored systems.

AI.tldr: The authors identify an exactly solvable class of continuously monitored systems (polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, homodyne measurement) and derive exact finite-dimensional stochastic representations for conditional quadrature moments, achieving Hilbert-space-dimension-independent computational complexity.
AI.motivation: Simulating nonlinear stochastic master equations is computationally challenging due to trajectory-level evolution of large Hilbert-space density matrices, especially for strongly nonlinear continuously monitored systems.
AI.method: The authors identify a solvable class of systems (polynomial single-quadrature Hamiltonians, linear damping, homodyne measurement of the same quadrature) and derive exact finite-dimensional stochastic representations for arbitrary finite-order quadrature moments via closure of the conditional momentum hierarchy, with complexity O(C_{d,n}T) independent of Hilbert-space dimension.
AI.result: The method requires no Fock-space truncation, Gaussian approximation, or moment closure approximation. Numerical simulations demonstrate agreement with direct stochastic master equation evolution, establishing an efficient exact method for studying nonlinear homodyne trajectories.
AI.conclusion: An exact, efficient computational method exists for a class of continuously monitored systems, with complexity independent of Hilbert-space dimension, enabling tractable simulation of nonlinear homodyne trajectories.

title: Qubit-qubit-qutrit quantum correlations in $H \to f \bar f V$
summary: We perform an extensive analysis of the quantum correlations carried by the qubit-qubit-qutrit pure state arising in the decay of a massive scalar into a fermion-antifermion pair and a massive gauge boson, $H \to f \bar f V$, specialising to the Higgs boson decay $h \to τ^- τ^+ Z$. Working with the exact tree-level spin state and its systematic expansion around the massless-fermion limit, we obtain analytic control over the entire phase space: the bipartite entanglement measures, the genuine $2 \otimes 2 \otimes 3$ entanglement structure (the Miyake classification), as well as the Bell-inequality violations and the non-stabiliserness (magic) are all mapped and reproduced by compact formulas. The bipartite measures exhibit a monogamy-like trade-off between the fermion pair and the fermion-boson pairs. The state is genuinely $2 \otimes 2 \otimes 3$ entangled over almost the entire phase space, most strongly in the collinear regions. We derive, for the first time, semi-analytical expressions for the tight $4 \times 4 \times 2$ Bell inequalities of the $2 \otimes 2 \otimes 3$ system, generalising the optimisation previously available only for three qubits, and find that the local-hidden-variable bound is violated over the entire phase space, reaching within a few per cent of the quantum bound at the upper endpoint of the di-tau mass spectrum. We further extend the stabiliser Rényi entropy and the non-local magic to systems with unequal local dimensions, and show that the near-endpoint state carries almost exactly one bit of non-local magic, which peaks at $\log_2 \frac{27}{7} \simeq 1.95$ in the collinear regions. The differential decay rate concentrates precisely in the most nonclassical region of the phase space.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes quantum correlations in a qubit-qubit-qutrit pure state from the decay $H \to f\bar{f} V$ (specifically $h \to \tau^-\tau^+ Z$), providing analytic formulas for bipartite entanglement, genuine $2\otimes2\otimes3$ entanglement (Miyake classification), Bell inequalities, and non-stabiliserness (magic) across the entire phase space. Key findings include a monogamy-like trade-off, genuine tripartite entanglement over almost all phase space, first semi-analytic expressions for $4\times4\times2$ Bell inequalities, and non-local magic peaking at $\log_2(27/7)\simeq 1.95$.
AI.motivation: To extend quantum information analysis to mixed-dimensional tripartite systems arising from realistic high-energy decays, and to map nonclassical correlations in Higgs boson decays with analytic control over the full phase space.
AI.method: Analysis of the exact tree-level spin state of $H\to f\bar{f}V$ with systematic expansion around the massless-fermion limit; derivation of bipartite entanglement measures, Miyake classification of $2\otimes2\otimes3$ entanglement, semi-analytic $4\times4\times2$ Bell inequalities, and stabiliser Rényi entropy extended to unequal local dimensions.
AI.result: Bipartite measures show monogamy-like trade-off; state is genuinely $2\otimes2\otimes3$ entangled over almost the entire phase space; Bell-inequality violations occur across the whole phase space; non-local magic peaks at $\log_2(27/7)\simeq 1.95$; differential decay rate concentrates in the most nonclassical region.
AI.conclusion: Higgs boson decays provide a rich laboratory for studying mixed-dimensional multipartite quantum correlations, with near-maximal nonclassicality achievable in specific kinematic regions.

title: Quantum Information Decoupling Beyond Finite Dimensions
summary: Quantum information decoupling is a pillar of quantum information theory, underlying quantum communication, error correction, and information recovery. However, its existing formulations rely on random unitary operations tied to finite-dimensional assumptions on quantum systems. Here we establish a decoupling framework for arbitrary separable, possibly infinite-dimensional systems. For finite-dimensional inputs and arbitrary separable reference/output systems, we derive error bounds on one-shot decoupling for completely positive maps in terms of sandwiched Rényi conditional entropies. For partial-trace decoupling with finite-dimensional references, the error exponent is optimal up to the known critical rate. To handle infinite-dimensional inputs, we assume finite entropy of the manipulated system. We construct finite-rank projections on independent and identically distributed (IID) states to restrict randomization to a projected finite-dimensional subspace, while ensuring high success probability by including auxiliary components in the discarded subsystem at asymptotically negligible cost. This leads to an infinite-dimensional IID partial-trace decoupling protocol achieving optimal asymptotic dimension rates. As an application, we construct an infinite-dimensional quantum-state-merging protocol, a mother protocol of quantum information theory. Under finite entropy of Alice's marginal, it achieves the same quantum-communication and total-cost rates as in finite dimensions, governed by mutual information and conditional entropy. These results show that the operational interpretation of entropic quantities through these achievable rates constitutes a universal principle beyond finite dimensions. More broadly, our framework provides foundational tools for exploring quantum information regardless of whether we model the physical world using finite- or infinite-dimensional spaces.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a quantum information decoupling framework for arbitrary separable (possibly infinite-dimensional) systems, deriving one-shot error bounds via sandwiched Rényi conditional entropies, achieving optimal asymptotic rates for IID partial-trace decoupling, and demonstrating applications such as infinite-dimensional quantum-state merging with rates matching finite-dimensional operational interpretations.
AI.motivation: Existing decoupling formulations rely on random unitary operations and finite-dimensional assumptions. The authors aim to extend decoupling theory to infinite-dimensional systems, which is essential for a complete operational understanding of quantum information theory beyond finite dimensions.
AI.method: The authors use finite-rank projections on IID states to restrict randomization to a projected finite-dimensional subspace, adding auxiliary components in the discarded subsystem at asymptotically negligible cost, and derive error bounds using sandwiched Rényi conditional entropies.
AI.result: Error bounds for one-shot decoupling of completely positive maps; optimal error exponent for partial-trace decoupling up to the critical rate; optimal asymptotic dimension rates for infinite-dimensional IID partial-trace decoupling; a quantum-state-merging protocol achieving the same quantum-communication and total-cost rates as in finite dimensions under finite entropy of Alice's marginal.
AI.conclusion: The operational interpretation of entropic quantities through achievable rates is a universal principle beyond finite dimensions, providing foundational tools for exploring quantum information in both finite- and infinite-dimensional settings.

title: Linear Algebra of Generalized Contextuality in All Prepare-Transform-Measure Scenarios
comment: 28 pages, one figure, comments are welcome
summary: Generalized contextuality is a canonical distinguishing property of nonclassical generalized probabilistic theories, in particular quantum mechanics. Methods for certification and characterization of generalized contextuality of a given generalized probabilistic theory are well developed for prepare-measure and single-stage prepare-transform-measure scenarios. In a recent work [arXiv:2512.10000], a bottom-up, statistics-first linear-algebraic framework for contextuality in prepare-measure scenarios was introduced. We extend this approach to operational scenarios with sequential transformations with an arbitrary number of stages. We give a full decision procedure for contextuality of such scenarios within operational theories and analyze its computational complexity. In particular, our decision procedure has a complexity linearly exponential in the minimum generalized probabilistic theory (GPT) dimension, and polynomial in the number of procedures. We demonstrate our framework and approach through multiple examples, including Spekkens' toy theory and the 8-state single-qubit stabilizer theory. In particular, we construct an operational theory in which contextuality manifests itself only in the sequential structure of the transformations. Our findings thus shed new light on the significant role of compositional structures in the phenomenon of generalized contextuality.

AI.tldr: This paper extends a statistics-first linear-algebraic framework for generalized contextuality from prepare-measure scenarios to multi-stage sequential transformation scenarios, providing a full decision procedure with complexity exponential in minimum GPT dimension and polynomial in number of procedures.
AI.motivation: To extend the framework for generalized contextuality from simple prepare-measure scenarios to more complex operational scenarios involving sequential transformations with an arbitrary number of stages.
AI.method: A bottom-up, statistics-first linear-algebraic framework is extended to sequential transformation scenarios. A full decision procedure for contextuality is developed, with analysis of computational complexity. The framework is demonstrated on Spekkens' toy theory and the 8-state single-qubit stabilizer theory.
AI.result: The decision procedure has complexity linearly exponential in minimum GPT dimension and polynomial in the number of procedures. An operational theory is constructed where contextuality manifests only in the sequential structure of transformations.
AI.conclusion: Compositional structures play a significant role in generalized contextuality, as contextuality can emerge solely from sequential transformation structures rather than from individual stages.

title: State preparation and detection for quantum simulation of particle collisions
summary: Simulating the real-time dynamics of particle collisions is a promising application of quantum simulators, because classical methods such as tensor networks struggle to capture the highly entangled states generated in high-energy scattering. Realizing such simulations requires both the preparation of incoming wave packets and the detection of the outgoing scattering products. In this work, we propose protocols that address both challenges on programmable analog and digital quantum simulation platforms. Our state-preparation scheme uses a weakly coupled auxiliary qubit - or, more generally, a customized local quench - to inject a single quasiparticle with well-defined momentum. Because it relies only on conservation of energy, this scheme requires no fine-tuning or prior knowledge about particle eigenstates, making it robust against errors in calibration and implementation. The momenta of scattering products are then extracted, using only local measurements, from the interference pattern that arises when particles are reflected at the system's boundary. We validate our protocols through numerical simulations, first in a simple single-particle model and subsequently in two interacting many-body systems: a Rydberg atom chain and an Ising chain in a mixed field. We demonstrate how high-energy regimes, necessary to access inelastic scattering processes, can be reached through an adiabatic ramp, and how the wave packet shape can be optimized by spatially modulating the Hamiltonian. Finally, we show how the protocol can be generalized to systems with more than one spatial dimension. Our proposal provides a versatile approach to the quantum simulation of scattering phenomena, and is compatible with several quantum simulation platforms that are already experimentally available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes protocols for quantum simulation of particle collision dynamics, including state preparation using weakly coupled auxiliary qubits (or local quenches) to inject single quasiparticles with well-defined momentum, and detection of scattering products via interference patterns from boundary reflections using only local measurements. The methods are validated on single-particle, Rydberg atom chain, and Ising chain models.
AI.motivation: Simulating real-time dynamics of particle collisions is a promising application of quantum simulators, but classical methods like tensor networks struggle with highly entangled states in high-energy scattering. Both preparing incoming wave packets and detecting outgoing scattering products remain challenging.
AI.method: The authors propose a state-preparation scheme using a weakly coupled auxiliary qubit (or customized local quench) to inject a single quasiparticle with well-defined momentum, relying only on energy conservation (no fine-tuning required). Detection extracts momenta of scattering products from interference patterns when particles reflect at system boundaries, using only local measurements. They also use adiabatic ramps for high-energy regimes and spatially modulated Hamiltonians for wave packet optimization.
AI.result: Protocols validated through numerical simulations in a simple single-particle model, a Rydberg atom chain, and an Ising chain in a mixed field. Demonstrated access to high-energy inelastic scattering regimes and wave packet shape optimization. Protocol generalizable to systems with more than one spatial dimension.
AI.conclusion: The proposal provides a versatile approach to quantum simulation of scattering phenomena, compatible with several experimentally available quantum simulation platforms.

title: Contextual advantage implies limited distinguishability in any physical theory
summary: A central question in quantum information is whether a given set of states can provide an advantage in some information-processing task. We establish a universal connection between two such questions: how well a set of states can be discriminated, and whether it can power tasks whose advantage stems from generalized contextuality. Working in the framework of generalized probabilistic theories (GPTs), which includes quantum and classical systems as special cases, we show that any set of states able to provide a nonclassical advantage in a contextuality-powered task must obey nontrivial upper bounds on the success probability of every state discrimination task using the full set. Contextual advantage therefore implies limited distinguishability, exposing a trade-off between two basic operational resources. Importantly, this is more than a statement about the idealized limit: perfect distinguishability is not needed to preclude contextuality. Our thresholds lie strictly below unity, so any set whose discrimination performance exceeds them while still imperfectly distinguishable is already guaranteed to admit a noncontextual explanation. The bounds follow from a simple geometric property, linear dependence of the state set, take a closed analytical form, and depend only on the prior of the task and the convex geometry of the states. As an illustration, we apply them to generalized parity-oblivious multiplexing, where sufficiently high success in the task implies that at least one sub-ensemble of the codebook cannot power any contextual advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a universal trade-off between state distinguishability and contextual advantage in generalized probabilistic theories: any set of states that provides a nonclassical contextual advantage must have limited success in state discrimination tasks, with bounds that are strictly below unity and derived from the linear dependence of the state set.
AI.motivation: To understand whether a given set of quantum states can provide an advantage in information-processing tasks, specifically by connecting two fundamental questions: state discrimination ability and the presence of generalized contextuality.
AI.method: Working within the GPT framework (including quantum and classical systems), the authors derive geometric bounds based on linear dependence of the state set, providing closed-form analytical thresholds that depend only on the task prior and convex geometry of the states.
AI.result: Contextual advantage implies limited distinguishability; the bounds are strictly below unity, meaning even imperfectly distinguishable sets can be guaranteed noncontextual if their discrimination performance exceeds certain thresholds.
AI.conclusion: A universal trade-off exists between two basic operational resources—state distinguishability and contextual advantage—with applications to tasks like parity-oblivious multiplexing where high success precludes contextual advantage in at least one sub-ensemble.

title: Lindbladian quantization of mechanical systems with nonholonomic constraints
summary: Nonholonomic mechanics describes systems subject to non-integrable velocity constraints, such as rolling bodies and skating motion. These systems generally lack a canonical Hamiltonian formulation, obstructing standard quantization methods. Here we quantize nonholonomic systems as Markovian open quantum systems, with the nonholonomic constraint appearing in a large-dissipation limit. We find explicit Lindblad superoperators that reproduce the classical dynamics of the Chaplygin sleigh and the Suslov problem in the semiclassical limit. The master equation is numerically simulated, and the covariance is shown to satisfy a relation predicted by the theory of metastability in open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a novel quantization approach for nonholonomic mechanical systems using Markovian open quantum system theory, where nonholonomic constraints emerge in a large-dissipation limit. The authors derive Lindblad superoperators that reproduce classical dynamics for the Chaplygin sleigh and Suslov problem in the semiclassical limit, and validate their results through numerical simulation of the master equation.
AI.motivation: Nonholonomic mechanics lacks a canonical Hamiltonian formulation, which obstructs standard quantization methods. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing a quantization framework applicable to systems with non-integrable velocity constraints.
AI.method: The authors quantize nonholonomic systems as Markovian open quantum systems, imposing the nonholonomic constraint through a large-dissipation limit. They derive explicit Lindblad superoperators for the Chaplygin sleigh and Suslov problem, and numerically simulate the resulting master equation.
AI.result: The derived Lindblad superoperators reproduce classical dynamics in the semiclassical limit. Numerical simulations show the covariance satisfies a relation predicted by metastability theory in open quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: Nonholonomic systems can be consistently quantized via open quantum system formalism with constrained dynamics emerging in the strong-dissipation regime, validated by agreement with metastability theory.

title: Graph Theoretic Approach to Quantum Nonstabilizerness
summary: Detecting nonstabilizerness requires full tomography and an optimization over exponentially many stabilizer states. A limited Pauli measurement set promises resource-efficient magic certification, yet the resulting reduced stabilizer polytope is generally difficult to characterize. We trace this difficulty into two coupled obstructions: the simultaneous measurability of measurements captured by their frustration graph structure, and the consistency of sign dependencies from stabilizer formalism. We show that the sign dependencies can be discarded exactly whenever active dependencies are absent, and that perfect frustration graphs then make this reduced polytope efficiently solvable. This solvable regime derives a closed form bounded by the clique number of the frustration graph, revealing a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability. Clifford covariance allows rotated measurement sets to enlarge the detectable state space without raising the capacity. Graph structure therefore emerges as both a certificate of tractability and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the difficulty of magic state detection stems from two coupled obstructions: measurement frustration graphs and stabilizer sign dependencies. When sign dependencies are absent and the frustration graph is perfect, the reduced stabilizer polytope becomes efficiently solvable, yielding a closed-form bound tied to the graph's clique number. This reveals a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability, with Clifford covariance enabling expanded detectable state space without increased capacity. Graph structure thus serves as both a tractability certificate and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection.
AI.motivation: Magic (nonstabilizerness) detection is crucial for quantum computing but requires full tomography and optimization over exponentially many stabilizer states. Using limited Pauli measurement sets could enable resource-efficient certification, but the resulting reduced stabilizer polytope is typically hard to characterize. The authors aim to identify the fundamental obstructions to this characterization and find regimes where it becomes tractable.
AI.method: The paper decomposes the difficulty into two obstructions: (1) the frustration graph structure of measurements (capturing simultaneous measurability), and (2) sign dependencies from stabilizer formalism. It shows that when active sign dependencies are absent, the sign constraints can be discarded. For perfect frustration graphs, the reduced polytope becomes efficiently solvable, yielding a closed-form solution bounded by the graph's clique number. Clifford covariance is used to rotate measurement sets for expanded detectability.
AI.result: A closed-form bound for magic detection derived from the clique number of the frustration graph; demonstration of a tradeoff between witness capacity and simultaneous measurability; Clifford covariance enables rotating measurement sets to enlarge detectable state space without increasing capacity.
AI.conclusion: Graph structure (frustration graphs) serves as both a certificate of computational tractability and a design principle for scalable magic resource detection, offering a way to balance witness capacity and measurement feasibility.

title: Role of flavor degrees of freedom in quantum simulations of disorder-free localization
summary: A recent \texttt{Google Quantum AI} experiment [\href{https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adr9680}{Gyawali \textit{et al.}, Science \textbf{393}, 71 (2026)}] has exploited quantum parallelism to emulate disorder-averaged many-body dynamics, with conserved local degrees of freedom generating an effective disorder potential. We investigate how the local spectrum of these static variables controls localization in a flavor-extended ${\mathbb Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory, which maps onto a mixed-field Ising chain with $n$-level bond disorder. Combining finite-size spectral and entanglement diagnostics with infinite matrix-product state dynamics, we find a qualitative distinction between binary and multilevel disorder. For $n=2$, apparent localization ultimately gives way to thermalization; the long-lived transient arises from energy-scale separation, degenerate spectral towers, and approximate Hilbert-space fragmentation. By contrast, $n=4$ displays consistent localization signatures, including Poissonian level statistics, area-law eigenstate entanglement, nonthermal entanglement spectra, and persistent local memory over accessible times in the thermodynamic limit. Our results show that, despite its larger variance, binary disorder lacks the local amplitude diversity needed to suppress resonances. Thus, localization is governed not simply by disorder strength, but by the local disorder spectrum and the resulting resonant connectivity of the many-body Hilbert space.

AI.tldr: The paper studies localization in a flavor-extended Z₂ lattice gauge theory mapped to a mixed-field Ising chain with n-level bond disorder. It finds that binary disorder (n=2) only yields transient localization that eventually thermalizes, while multilevel disorder (n=4) shows robust localization signatures including Poissonian statistics, area-law entanglement, and persistent local memory. Localization is governed not by disorder strength alone but by the local disorder spectrum and resonant Hilbert-space connectivity.
AI.motivation: To understand how the local spectrum of static degrees of freedom controls localization in many-body quantum systems, particularly in the context of a Google Quantum AI experiment that emulates disorder-averaged dynamics via quantum parallelism.
AI.method: The authors map a flavor-extended Z₂ lattice gauge theory onto a mixed-field Ising chain with n-level bond disorder. They combine finite-size spectral analysis, entanglement diagnostics (e.g., level statistics, eigenstate entanglement entropy, entanglement spectra), and infinite matrix-product state dynamics to compare binary (n=2) and multilevel (n=4) disorder.
AI.result: Binary disorder (n=2) exhibits only apparent localization with a long-lived transient, ultimately thermalizing due to energy-scale separation, degenerate spectral towers, and approximate Hilbert-space fragmentation. Multilevel disorder (n=4) shows genuine localization: Poissonian level statistics, area-law entanglement entropy, nonthermal entanglement spectra, and persistent local memory over accessible timescales in the thermodynamic limit.
AI.conclusion: Localization is not solely determined by disorder strength but critically depends on the local disorder spectrum and the resulting resonant connectivity of the many-body Hilbert space. Binary disorder, despite larger variance, lacks the local amplitude diversity needed to suppress resonances.

title: Algebraic paradoxes in adaptive quantum computation
summary:
Measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) is a universal model of quantum computation whose full power requires adaptivity. Contextuality is known to power quantum advantage in MBQC, yet it has resisted algebraic analysis in the adaptive setting.
  We show that if an adaptive $\mathbb{Z}_2$-linear measurement-based quantum computing protocol deterministically computes a non-affine Boolean function, then the underlying quantum resource satisfies an inconsistent set of linear equations. This witnesses an algebraic form of strong contextuality generalising Mermin's All-versus-Nothing arguments. Such algebraic contextuality can be detected cohomologically, resolving an open question posed by Raussendorf, who had established cohomological witnesses of contextuality for non-adaptive protocols, but left the adaptive case open. We prove this result constructively: we model adaptive measurement protocols as ordinary measurements on a larger scenario of tree-like measurements, and explicitly build the inconsistent equations inductively.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that adaptive $\mathbb{Z}_2$-linear MBQC protocols deterministically computing non-affine Boolean functions exhibit algebraic contextuality (generalizing Mermin's All-versus-Nothing arguments), which can be detected cohomologically—resolving an open question by Raussendorf.
AI.motivation: To extend cohomological contextuality detection from non-adaptive to adaptive measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC), addressing a long-standing open problem about whether algebraic contextuality can be witnessed in adaptive settings.
AI.method: Models adaptive measurement protocols as ordinary measurements on a larger scenario with tree-like measurements, then explicitly constructs inconsistent linear equations inductively, showing resource states must satisfy a contradictory set of linear equations for deterministic computation of non-affine Boolean functions.
AI.result: Adaptive $\mathbb{Z}_2$-linear MBQC protocols that deterministically compute non-affine Boolean functions produce an inconsistent system of linear equations on the quantum resource, providing an algebraic witness of strong contextuality. This contextuality is detectable via cohomology.
AI.conclusion: Algebraic contextuality generalizing Mermin's All-versus-Nothing arguments exists in adaptive MBQC and can be detected cohomologically, closing the open question left by Raussendorf for the adaptive case.

title: A two-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducer
summary: Optical quantum networks provide a natural route for connecting distant superconducting quantum processors, enabling distributed quantum computation, sensing, and communication. Piezo-optomechanical transducers are among the leading candidates for scalable microwave-to-optical quantum interfaces. However, prior one-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducers remain limited by optical-absorption-induced heating and the resulting thermal noise. Two-dimensional optomechanical crystals offer substantially improved thermalization from better thermal anchoring, but their structural complexity has so far hindered the realization of a fully integrated two-dimensional transducer. Here, we overcome this challenge with a new design strategy based on band structure engineering. We fabricate the devices and experimentally characterize the response, measuring an electromechanical damping rate of 4.6 kHz at room temperature and electromechanical coupling rate of 0.17 MHz by wire-bonding to a multi-mode microwave resonator at 10 mK. Bidirectional transduction is performed with a calibrated internal efficiency of 0.85\% in the continuous-wave operation, alongside pulsed photon-phonon pair generation near its quantum ground state. Our results represent a significant step toward high-efficiency and low-noise transducers for entangling remote superconducting qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a two-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducer using band structure engineering to overcome thermal noise limitations of prior one-dimensional designs. The device achieves electromechanical damping of 4.6 kHz, coupling rate of 0.17 MHz, bidirectional transduction efficiency of 0.85%, and pulsed photon-phonon pair generation near the quantum ground state, advancing toward high-efficiency, low-noise quantum interfaces for connecting superconducting processors via optical networks.
AI.motivation: Prior one-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducers suffer from optical-absorption-induced heating and thermal noise. Although two-dimensional optomechanical crystals offer better thermal anchoring, their structural complexity has prevented fully integrated implementation.
AI.method: The authors employ a new design strategy based on band structure engineering to realize a fully integrated two-dimensional piezo-optomechanical transducer. They fabricate devices and wire-bond them to a multi-mode microwave resonator at 10 mK for characterization.
AI.result: Electromechanical damping rate of 4.6 kHz at room temperature; electromechanical coupling rate of 0.17 MHz at 10 mK; bidirectional transduction internal efficiency of 0.85% in continuous-wave operation; pulsed photon-phonon pair generation near the quantum ground state.
AI.conclusion: The results represent a significant step toward high-efficiency and low-noise transducers for entangling remote superconducting qubits, enabling distributed quantum computation, sensing, and communication via optical quantum networks.

title: Minimal Counterexamples of the MacWilliams Extension Theorem for Stabilizer Codes
summary: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for module alphabets with non-cyclic socle, and the label alphabet of qudit stabilizer codes, $\F_{q^2}$ over $\F_q$, is such an alphabet. Quantum error correction, however, only ever sees \emph{self-orthogonal} additive codes, and whether that rigidity rescues the theorem---equivalently, whether every weight-preserving isomorphism of stabilizer groups is implemented by local Cliffords and a qudit permutation---was asked by Gluesing-Luerssen and Pllaha and answered negatively by Pllaha for particular qubit codes. We develop the negative answer systematically and at the smallest possible scales. For every prime power $q$ we construct a pair of $[[q+1,q-1]]_q$ stabilizer codes and a weight-preserving isomorphism between them extending to no monomial transformation; the codespaces are inequivalent even under arbitrary local unitaries combined with permutations, though they share Shor--Laflamme enumerators. Self-orthogonality is automatic here, by two elementary lemmas which also show that Dyshko's threshold-length counterexamples were already self-orthogonal, unremarked. For qubits we prove by exhaustive search that length $3$ is minimal and the counterexample essentially unique. Dropping the ``idle qudit'' invariant that detects these, we find the minimal full-support lengths: $4$ for a non-extendable isometry, $5$ for a weight-isometric pair that is not monomially equivalent, realized by explicit $[[5,2]]$ codes; at length $6$ all nontrivial stabilizer elements can have weight $\ge 4$. Whether these codespaces are locally unitarily equivalent is posed as an open problem, connecting the extension problem to the LU--LC circle of questions.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically studies the failure of the MacWilliams extension theorem for qudit stabilizer codes over F_{q^2}/F_q, constructing explicit counterexamples at minimal lengths where weight-preserving isomorphisms of stabilizer groups cannot be extended to monomial transformations or local unitaries.
AI.motivation: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for module alphabets with non-cyclic socle, including the label alphabet F_{q^2}/F_q used in qudit stabilizer codes. It was an open question whether restricting to self-orthogonal additive codes (as in quantum error correction) rescues the theorem, i.e., whether every weight-preserving isomorphism of stabilizer groups is implemented by local Cliffords and a qudit permutation. This paper aims to answer this negatively and systematically.
AI.method: The authors construct explicit pairs of [[q+1, q-1]]_q stabilizer codes for every prime power q, with a weight-preserving isomorphism that extends to no monomial transformation. They use two elementary lemmas showing self-orthogonality is automatic. For qubits, exhaustive search finds minimal length 3 is necessary and the counterexample is essentially unique. They also find minimal full-support lengths: 4 for a non-extendable isometry, 5 for a weight-isometric pair not monomially equivalent (explicit [[5,2]] codes).
AI.result: The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for qudit stabilizer codes even with self-orthogonality. Explicit counterexamples exist at length q+1 for any prime power q, with codespaces inequivalent under local unitaries and permutations despite sharing Shor-Laflamme enumerators. For qubits, length 3 is minimal; full-support counterexamples appear at lengths 4 and 5.
AI.conclusion: Self-orthogonality does not rescue the MacWilliams extension theorem for stabilizer codes. The paper raises an open problem about whether the constructed codespaces are locally unitarily equivalent, connecting to the LU-LC circle of questions.

title: Supermartingales in Quantum Resources Theories: Where do quantum resources go when you're watching?
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures (+ 2 pages, 1 figure of Appendix + 8 pages of Supp. Mat.)
summary: We establish a connection between quantum resource theory and probability theory, under repeated application of free operations. We show that strong monotonicity of a resource measure implies that the resource is a supermartingale. We then use the optional stopping and martingale convergence theorems to derive bounds on the efficiency of post-selection, and other free adaptive strategies. We also describe the asymptotic dynamics of the conditional state, where resource fluctuations are necessarily absent, showing one of two distinct phenomena occurs: resource vanishing or resource freezing.

AI.tldr: This paper connects quantum resource theory with probability theory, showing that strong monotonicity of a resource measure implies it is a supermartingale under repeated free operations. Using martingale theorems, it derives bounds on post-selection efficiency and other adaptive strategies, and describes the asymptotic dynamics of conditional states where resource fluctuations vanish, leading to either resource vanishing or freezing.
AI.motivation: To bridge quantum resource theory and probability theory, specifically to understand the dynamical behavior of quantum resources under repeated free operations and to derive general bounds on the efficiency of post-selection and adaptive strategies.
AI.method: The authors establish a connection by showing that strong monotonicity implies the resource measure is a supermartingale. They apply the optional stopping theorem and martingale convergence theorems from probability theory to analyze resource dynamics under repeated free operations.
AI.result: Bounds on the efficiency of post-selection and free adaptive strategies are derived. The asymptotic dynamics of the conditional state are characterized, showing two possible distinct phenomena: resource vanishing or resource freezing, with fluctuations necessarily absent in the limit.
AI.conclusion: The martingale framework provides a powerful tool for analyzing quantum resource theories under repeated operations, yielding fundamental limits on resource manipulation and a classification of asymptotic resource behavior.

title: Precise 2D electric field density simulations for superconducting quantum devices
summary: Dielectric loss due to two-level systems is a limiting factor for superconducting qubit relaxation times. These losses arise mostly from nanometer-scale interfacial defect regions in superconducting devices with planar dimensions of microns to millimeters, thus making it resource intensive to accurately simulate the electric field density in these regions with traditional electromagnetic solvers. In this work, we demonstrate a fast boundary integral equation solver that allows precise simulation of electric field density in these thin regions, showing a speedup of around two orders of magnitude over traditional solvers, with relative errors around $10^{-7}$ for a ten-minute solution runtime. By computing participation ratios through Green's first identity without squaring the electric field, our approach is less susceptible to the field singularities near conductor corners. We apply this solver to a basic untrenched coplanar waveguide cross-section, showing that the common assumption of participation ratio linearity with dielectric constant holds well for some interfaces and not others; in particular, while the metal-air (MA) top and corner follow this linear relationship strongly, the MA sidewall does not. We then compare isotropic and anisotropic etching, showing that the MA sidewall and the metal-air-substrate triple junction are the most strongly affected. We are currently leveraging this solver to explore geometries that will uniquely isolate the participation ratios of the different dielectrics. Finally, we are working to combine this solver framework with a full 3D microwave solver to accurately calculate participation ratios for the thin dielectrics that are known sources of loss in superconducting qubits.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fast boundary integral equation solver for simulating electric field density in thin interfacial regions of superconducting qubits, achieving ~100× speedup over traditional methods with high accuracy (relative errors ~10⁻⁷). Using Green's first identity to compute participation ratios avoids field singularities at conductor corners. Application to coplanar waveguide cross-sections reveals that the linearity assumption between participation ratio and dielectric constant holds for some interfaces (metal-air top, corner) but not others (metal-air sidewall). Isotropic vs. anisotropic etching comparisons show metal-air sidewalls and triple junctions are most affected.
AI.motivation: Dielectric loss from two-level systems in nanometer-scale interfacial defect regions limits superconducting qubit relaxation times. Simulating electric field density in these thin regions using traditional electromagnetic solvers is resource-intensive due to the scale mismatch (nanometer defects vs. micron-to-millimeter planar dimensions).
AI.method: A fast boundary integral equation solver is developed for precise simulation of electric field density in thin interfacial regions. Participation ratios are computed via Green's first identity (avoiding squaring the electric field) to reduce susceptibility to field singularities near conductor corners.
AI.result: ~100× speedup over traditional solvers with relative errors ~10⁻⁷ in ten minutes. The linearity assumption between participation ratio and dielectric constant holds well for MA top and corner interfaces but fails for the MA sidewall. Isotropic vs. anisotropic etching most strongly affects the MA sidewall and the metal-air-substrate triple junction.
AI.conclusion: The solver enables efficient and accurate analysis of thin dielectric losses. Future work includes exploring geometries to isolate participation ratios of different dielectrics and combining the solver framework with a full 3D microwave solver.

title: Optimal Interaction Free Localization with Multipath Interferometers
summary: Interaction-free measurement (IFM) certifies the presence of an absorbing object without a photon ever being absorbed by it. When several candidate locations are available, existing protocols can also identify which one holds the absorber, but they do so by testing paths sequentially through two-path interferometers, resolving a binary presence question at each step. We propose a different approach: probing all candidate locations at once, with the photon prepared in a coherent superposition across every path before a single measurement resolves the outcome. We prove that a three-stage protocol built on a $d$-path interferometer attains the exact one-shot optimum for this task, and we extend it to $k$ absorbers among $d$ paths, where the no-absorption branch encodes the entire absorber subset coherently rather than revealing individual locations one by one. The dark port therefore ceases to be a mere witness of presence and becomes a location-resolving signal. We then move beyond single-pass strategies using the quantum-comb formalism, casting the problem as an exact optimization over all multi-pass strategies and showing that adaptive protocols surpass the one-shot ceiling. Enriching the interferometer geometry with one additional path guaranteed to be empty, we show that sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation all become particular feasible strategies within this same optimization, rather than separate benchmarks to compare against. This unified formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for any given set of resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging protocols for the study of fragile, absorption-sensitive samples.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new interaction-free measurement (IFM) protocol that probes all candidate absorber locations simultaneously using a $d$-path interferometer with coherent superposition, achieving exact one-shot optimum for locating absorbers. It extends to $k$ absorbers among $d$ paths, uses quantum-comb formalism to optimize multi-pass adaptive strategies, and unifies sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation within a single optimization framework for loss-resilient quantum imaging.
AI.motivation: Existing IFM protocols for locating absorbers among multiple candidates test paths sequentially through two-path interferometers, resolving a binary presence question at each step. The authors aim to overcome this sequential limitation by probing all candidate locations simultaneously, enabling more efficient interaction-free localization.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-stage protocol built on a $d$-path interferometer where the photon is prepared in a coherent superposition across all paths before a single measurement. They prove it attains the one-shot optimum. They extend to $k$ absorbers among $d$ paths, where the no-absorption branch encodes the entire absorber subset coherently. They then apply the quantum-comb formalism to optimize over all multi-pass adaptive strategies, enriching the geometry with an additional empty reference path.
AI.result: The proposed protocol achieves the exact one-shot optimum for interaction-free localization. The dark port becomes a location-resolving signal rather than a mere presence witness. Adaptive multi-pass strategies surpass the one-shot ceiling. Sequential scanning, bright-port recycling, and Zeno-type interrogation are shown to be specific feasible strategies within the same unified optimization framework.
AI.conclusion: The unified quantum-comb-based formulation identifies the optimal interaction-free localization strategy for any given set of resources, opening a route toward loss-resilient quantum imaging protocols for studying fragile, absorption-sensitive samples.

title: Hardware-Aware QUBO Reformulation of Constrained Binary Optimization via the Walsh-Fourier Transform
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE 2026). Code: https://github.com/lklee9/topology-aware-walsh-fourier-penalization
summary: We present a novel slack-free, penalty-based framework for reformulating constrained binary optimization as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) on near-term quantum annealing hardware. Given a user-chosen penalty function that most naturally captures a constraint---typically non-quadratic, such as a Heaviside-function surrogate---and a target probability measure over the Boolean hypercube, our method returns the weighted least-squares projection of the chosen penalty function onto the subspace spanned by linear and quadratic Walsh--Fourier characters that correspond to physically realizable couplings on the target hardware graph. Within this restricted family, the resulting quadratic surrogate is uniquely and optimally determined by the normal equations: unlike state-of-the-art approaches, it introduces no per-constraint penalty coefficients to tune and avoids dense all-pairs couplings by construction. Two practical consequences follow. First, the projected penalty respects device connectivity, reducing chain lengths and physical-qubit overhead after minor embedding. Second, we show empirically that this hardware-native surrogate can outperform denser full-pairwise projections, despite being drawn from a strictly smaller approximation space. This advantage widens once the QUBO is embedded and sampled on quantum annealers, yielding samples with the lowest worst-case and mean objective gaps compared to unbalanced penalization and a hardware-blind projection onto all quadratic terms.

AI.tldr: A slack-free, penalty-based framework that projects user-chosen (non-quadratic) penalty functions onto quadratic Walsh-Fourier characters realizable on the target quantum hardware graph, producing uniquely determined QUBO surrogates without per-constraint tuning or dense couplings.
AI.motivation: To reformulate constrained binary optimization as QUBO for near-term quantum annealers without introducing penalty coefficients to tune and without requiring dense all-pairs couplings that are costly to embed.
AI.method: Weighted least-squares projection of a user-chosen penalty function onto the subspace spanned by linear and quadratic Walsh-Fourier characters that correspond to physically realizable couplings on the target hardware graph, solved via normal equations.
AI.result: The hardware-native quadratic surrogate reduces chain lengths and qubit overhead after embedding, and empirically outperforms denser full-pairwise projections and unbalanced penalization, yielding lower worst-case and mean objective gaps on quantum annealers.
AI.conclusion: Projecting penalties onto hardware-realizable quadratic couplings is both feasible and advantageous; restricting approximations to a smaller, device-native space can improve solution quality over hardware-blind or dense alternatives.

title: On $R$-parastatistics I: Foundation
summary: Parastatistics is an exotic type of exchange statistics beyond fermions and bosons. Paraparticles transform in higher dimensional representations of the exchange symmetry group, analogous to non-Abelian anyons, yet consistently defined in any dimension. Although paraparticles have long been proposed, they were widely believed to be physically equivalent to fermions or bosons. Nevertheless, a recent paper proposed a different theory, called $R$-parastatistics, and demonstrated that nontrivial $R$-paraparticles can emerge as quasiparticles in condensed matter systems, and are observably distinct from both fermions and bosons. This paper develops the theoretical foundation and several extensions of $R$-parastatistics, with particular emphasis on its observable consequences. Central to this paper is a general theory of local observables extending the basic family introduced before. First, we define local observables that distinguish particle types. Second, we formulate local observables at special point defects that probe the internal indices of $R$-paraparticles, crucial for observing $R$-parastatistics and for the proposed applications in quantum information. Third, we introduce local observables that create or annihilate particle-antiparticle pairs, important for building a relativistic quantum field theory for $R$-paraparticles. We further introduce generalized hidden symmetries that act on internal indices of $R$-paraparticles while preserving the local observable algebra, providing a basis for proving local indistinguishability and for connecting to a categorical description of $R$-paraparticles. This work sets a solid theoretical foundation for understanding the fundamental physical properties of $R$-paraparticles and pave the way for finding them in nature.

AI.tldr: This paper develops the theoretical foundation for R-parastatistics—an exotic type of exchange statistics beyond fermions and bosons—by formulating local observables that distinguish particle types, probe internal indices at point defects, create/annihilate particle-antiparticle pairs, and introducing generalized hidden symmetries, establishing a framework for understanding and detecting R-paraparticles in condensed matter and quantum information applications.
AI.motivation: Despite long-standing theoretical proposals, paraparticles were believed to be physically equivalent to fermions or bosons. Recent work showed that nontrivial R-paraparticles can emerge as quasiparticles with observable distinctions, motivating the need for a solid theoretical foundation to understand their fundamental physical properties and guide experimental discovery.
AI.method: The paper develops a general theory of local observables extending a previously introduced basic family, including: (1) observables distinguishing particle types, (2) observables at special point defects probing internal indices of R-paraparticles, (3) observables creating/annihilating particle-antiparticle pairs, and (4) generalized hidden symmetries acting on internal indices while preserving the local observable algebra, connecting to a categorical description.
AI.result: A comprehensive theoretical framework for R-parastatistics is established, including a full set of local observables for particle type discrimination, point defect probing, pair creation/annihilation, and hidden symmetries that provide a basis for proving local indistinguishability and linking to categorical descriptions.
AI.conclusion: This work sets a solid theoretical foundation for understanding the fundamental physical properties of R-paraparticles and paves the way for finding them in nature, with implications for condensed matter physics and quantum information applications.

title: The Klein-Gordon-Fock theory as a one-particle relativistic quantum mechanics
summary: The Klein-Gordon-Fock (KGF) theory with scalar and vector potentials is presented as a one particle relativistic quantum mechanics (QM). First, the KGF equation is written in a Hamiltonian form, in spinor space; unlike the Feshbach-Villars approach, the Hamiltonian here is strictly Hermitian. Then this equation is rewritten for a one-component wave function. Expressions for the Hamiltonian and other observables' operators acting in the space of one-component wave functions are presented. The nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic limits of these expressions are considered. A general solution to the KGF equation describing a free particle is presented.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Klein-Gordon-Fock theory as a one-particle relativistic quantum mechanics, formulating it with a strictly Hermitian Hamiltonian in spinor space and deriving one-component wave function operators for various observables.
AI.motivation: To reformulate the KGF theory with scalar and vector potentials as a consistent one-particle relativistic quantum mechanics, addressing Hermiticity issues present in previous approaches like the Feshbach-Villars formalism.
AI.method: The KGF equation is first written in Hamiltonian form in spinor space with a strictly Hermitian Hamiltonian (unlike the Feshbach-Villars approach). It is then rewritten for a one-component wave function, with expressions for Hamiltonian and other observable operators derived. Nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic limits are examined, and a general free-particle solution is presented.
AI.result: A Hermitian Hamiltonian formulation of the KGF theory in spinor space, along with corresponding one-component wave function operators and their limiting behaviors in nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic regimes.
AI.conclusion: The KGF theory can be consistently formulated as a one-particle relativistic quantum mechanics with a strictly Hermitian Hamiltonian, offering an alternative to the Feshbach-Villars framework.

title: Molecular triplets and other metastable states for excitonic quantum batteries
comment: 26 pages, 5 figures. Submitted as Chapter 4 in Springer series: Advances in Atoms and Single Molecule Machines Vol. 17: Single Atom (molecule) Energy Storage: Towards a quantum battery. Editor: Christian Joachim. Comments and feedback are welcome
summary: Excitonic quantum batteries, based on organic fluorescent molecules embedded in optical microcavities, offer a room-temperature platform for studying collective effects in energy storage and developing applications. Recent experiments have offered evidence of superabsorption, a collective enhancement to the light absorption rate of organic molecules which leads to a scalable power density. However, they have also highlighted the challenge posed by rapid radiative decay of fluorescent molecules, which limits the energy storage lifetime. Current strategies to overcome this trade-off focus on controlling the coupling between the absorbing manifold and that used for energy storage. In this chapter, we review three implementations of this design principle: transferring energy from optically excited states to long-lived dark triplet states, generating triplet pairs and higher-spin states through singlet exciton fission, and forming charge-separated states. We discuss each mechanism from both theoretical and experimental perspectives, with particular emphasis on recent device implementations that have extended storage times by several orders of magnitude. We conclude with a cross-platform outlook on the role of metastable states across coherent and room-temperature implementations, from neutral atom arrays to masers and colour centres.

AI.tldr: This chapter reviews excitonic quantum batteries using organic fluorescent molecules in optical microcavities, focusing on strategies to overcome the trade-off between superabsorption (collective light absorption enhancement) and rapid radiative decay that limits energy storage lifetime. Three approaches are examined: transferring energy to dark triplet states, singlet exciton fission for triplet pairs/higher-spin states, and forming charge-separated states. Recent devices have extended storage times by orders of magnitude, with a cross-platform outlook on metastable states across various quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To address the fundamental trade-off in excitonic quantum batteries between superabsorption (collective enhancement of light absorption) and the rapid radiative decay of fluorescent molecules that severely limits energy storage lifetime, by exploring mechanisms that decouple absorption from storage.
AI.method: The chapter reviews three design strategies: (1) transferring energy from optically excited states to long-lived dark triplet states, (2) generating triplet pairs and higher-spin states via singlet exciton fission, and (3) forming charge-separated states. Each mechanism is analyzed from both theoretical and experimental perspectives, with emphasis on recent device implementations.
AI.result: Recent device implementations have successfully extended storage times by several orders of magnitude by employing metastable states (dark triplets, triplet pairs from fission, charge-separated states) that decouple the absorbing manifold from the storage manifold.
AI.conclusion: The cross-platform outlook suggests that metastable states play a crucial role across coherent and room-temperature implementations, from neutral atom arrays to masers and colour centres, indicating a general design principle for quantum battery systems.

title: Quantum Optical Reinforcement Learning via Spectrum-Resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel Interference
summary: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference-based optical neural networks can offer complexity advantages on benchmark learning tasks, but conventional readout compresses the coincidence spectrum into a single scalar, limiting its use in complex settings such as continuous-action reinforcement learning. Here we introduce a spectrum-resolved HOM (SR-HOM) architecture that promotes the photons' spectral degrees of freedom to a trainable computational resource and use it to construct a compact optical actor-critic agent. Diagonal spectral responses generate continuous actions, while higher-order spectral correlations provide nonlinear state-action features for value estimation. Across five continuous-control benchmarks, SR-HOM outperforms parameter-matched multilayer-perceptron baselines, including a \(4.4\times\) improvement in sample efficiency and a \(74.0\%\) increase in best 100-episode moving-average return for LunarLanderContinuous-v3. Applied to online calibration of drifted tunable-coupler CZ and iSWAP gates for transmon qubits, simulations show it restores fidelities to \(0.9917\) and \(0.9952\) respectively, exceeding \(99.8\%\) of their drift-free calibrated values.
