AI.tldr: Introduces a spectrum-resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel (SR-HOM) architecture that uses spectral degrees of freedom as trainable computational resources for optical neural networks, enabling a compact optical actor-critic agent for continuous-action reinforcement learning that outperforms parameter-matched MLP baselines across continuous-control benchmarks and quantum gate calibration tasks.
AI.motivation: Conventional HOM interference-based optical neural networks compress the coincidence spectrum into a single scalar, limiting their applicability in complex settings like continuous-action reinforcement learning. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by promoting spectral degrees of freedom to a trainable computational resource.
AI.method: Proposes a spectrum-resolved HOM (SR-HOM) architecture where diagonal spectral responses generate continuous actions and higher-order spectral correlations provide nonlinear state-action features for value estimation, constructing a compact optical actor-critic agent.
AI.result: SR-HOM outperforms parameter-matched MLP baselines across five continuous-control benchmarks, achieving 4.4× improvement in sample efficiency and 74.0% increase in best 100-episode moving-average return for LunarLanderContinuous-v3. In quantum gate calibration simulations, it restores CZ and iSWAP gate fidelities to 0.9917 and 0.9952, exceeding 99.8% of drift-free calibrated values.
AI.conclusion: The spectrum-resolved HOM architecture effectively unlocks spectral degrees of freedom as a computational resource, enabling compact optical neural networks to tackle complex continuous-action reinforcement learning and quantum gate calibration tasks with superior performance.

title: Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics for Quantum Simulations
summary: We develop a framework for quantum simulations of lattice SU($N_c$) gauge theory with quarks. Staggered and Wilson lattice fermions are considered in two and three spatial dimensions and a theta angle is included in three dimensions. The physical, gauge-invariant Hilbert space is formulated in a representation basis, where gauge and fermionic degrees of freedom are encoded by irreducible representations of SU($N_c$) that tensor at each lattice site to contain a singlet. We discuss algorithms for simulating time evolution on quantum computers and carry out noiseless simulations of lattice quantum chromodynamics ($N_c=3$) on small lattices with up to 32 qubits, showcasing theta angle effects, hadronic states, string dynamics, and a baryon chemical potential for the first time in three spatial dimensions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework for quantum simulations of lattice SU(N_c) gauge theory with quarks, using staggered and Wilson fermions in 2D and 3D, with a theta angle in 3D. The physical Hilbert space is formulated in a representation basis where gauge and fermionic degrees of freedom are encoded by irreducible representations of SU(N_c). Noiseless simulations of lattice QCD (N_c=3) on lattices up to 32 qubits demonstrate theta angle effects, hadronic states, string dynamics, and baryon chemical potential in three spatial dimensions.
AI.motivation: To enable quantum simulations of non-perturbative phenomena in lattice gauge theories, particularly lattice QCD, by developing a framework that respects gauge invariance and can be implemented on quantum computers, going beyond previous work that was limited to lower dimensions or simpler gauge groups.
AI.method: The authors formulate the physical Hilbert space in a representation basis where gauge and fermionic degrees of freedom are encoded by irreducible representations of SU(N_c) that tensor at each lattice site to contain a singlet. They consider both staggered and Wilson lattice fermions in two and three spatial dimensions, include a theta angle in 3D, and discuss algorithms for simulating time evolution on quantum computers.
AI.result: Noiseless simulations of lattice QCD (N_c=3) on small lattices with up to 32 qubits were carried out, showcasing theta angle effects, hadronic states, string dynamics, and a baryon chemical potential for the first time in three spatial dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories with quarks in higher dimensions, demonstrating key physical phenomena including theta angle effects, hadrons, string dynamics, and baryon chemical potential on near-term quantum devices.

title: Phase Retrievability of Super Operators and Measurements
summary:
We continue the study of Phase Retrieval in the Quantum Information setting in the style of \cite{liu2023phase}, in a manner which is more general in two primary ways: (a) Instead of only pure states we consider also states (and positive semidefinite operators) of bounded rank, as is done in Quantum Tomography; (b) We consider general super operators instead of only quantum channels.
  We show that in order to have phase retrieval with respect to positive semidefinite operators of bounded rank, it suffices to discriminate between perfectly distinguishable pairs (i.e. those with orthogonal supports). From this we prove that phase retrievability is always Lipschitz stable with respect to the trace norm, and then we use the Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities to deduce stability with respect to the Bures--Wasserstein distance (thus generalizing the known stability results for phase retrieval in Frame Theory). For Hermitian-preserving super operators taking values in block-diagonal matrices, we characterize phase retrievability in terms of conditions inspired by the classical complement property from Frame Theory.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes Phase Retrieval in Quantum Information to bounded-rank positive semidefinite operators and general super operators, showing phase retrievability is Lipschitz stable under trace norm and Bures-Wasserstein distance, with a complement-property-based characterization for Hermitian-preserving super operators.
AI.motivation: To extend phase retrieval theory from pure quantum states to mixed states and bounded-rank positive semidefinite operators, and from quantum channels to general super operators, thereby bridging gaps between Phase Retrieval and Quantum Tomography.
AI.method: The paper shows that phase retrieval for bounded-rank PSD operators reduces to discriminating perfectly distinguishable pairs (orthogonal supports). It leverages Fuchs-van de Graaf inequalities to translate trace-norm stability to Bures-Wasserstein stability. For Hermitian-preserving super operators with block-diagonal output, it characterizes phase retrievability via a complement property analogous to Frame Theory.
AI.result: Phase retrievability is Lipschitz stable under trace norm, and consequently stable under Bures-Wasserstein distance. A complement-property-based characterization is provided for Hermitian-preserving super operators mapping to block-diagonal matrices.
AI.conclusion: The work unifies and generalizes known stability results from both Phase Retrieval (Frame Theory) and Quantum Tomography, offering a broader framework for quantum phase retrieval.

title: Finding diagonal logical gates in CSS codes and circuits
summary: Finding efficient schemes for non-Clifford logic or magic state preparation is one of the central challenges on the way to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Many of the proposed schemes rely on diagonal non-Clifford logical gates acting on CSS codes in space or decorating CSS-type syndrome-extraction circuits in spacetime. Here we propose and implement efficient algorithms to find all (spacetime) logical gates of a given CSS code (circuit) composed from a prescribed set of ansatz gates. Depending on the choice of ansatz gates, this means finding transversal gates, more general locality-preserving logical circuits, folding gates, or similar. While we focus on qubit diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, we also discuss the generalization to arbitrary diagonal non-hierarchy gates, certain non-diagonal gates, as well as prime and composite-dimensional qudits. Our method works by rephrasing code-space preserving gates as the kernel of the ``pullback'' of the $X$ check matrix onto phase functions, which maps between finite abelian 2-groups. We implement a fast ``filtration'' method to find this kernel. The runtime for finding fault-tolerant logical gates in a qLDPC code with $O(n)$ qubits or a circuit with $O(n)$ gates in a naive dense implementation is $O(n^3)$, with potential for improvement making use of sparsity.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes efficient algorithms to find all spacetime logical gates (transversal, locality-preserving, folding, etc.) of CSS codes/circuits by rephrasing code-space preserving gates as the kernel of a "pullback" of the X check matrix onto phase functions, using a fast filtration method with O(n³) runtime for qLDPC codes.
AI.motivation: Finding efficient schemes for non-Clifford logic or magic state preparation is a central challenge for fault-tolerant quantum computation, motivating the need for systematic methods to discover logical gates in CSS codes.
AI.method: The method rephrases code-space preserving gates as the kernel of a "pullback" of the X check matrix onto phase functions, mapping between finite abelian 2-groups. A fast "filtration" method is implemented to find this kernel. The approach works for qubit diagonal gates in the Clifford hierarchy, arbitrary diagonal non-hierarchy gates, some non-diagonal gates, and qudits of prime or composite dimensions.
AI.result: The runtime for finding fault-tolerant logical gates in a qLDPC code with O(n) qubits or a circuit with O(n) gates in a naive dense implementation is O(n³), with potential for improvement by exploiting sparsity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithms provide a systematic and efficient way to discover all spacetime logical gates for CSS codes from a prescribed ansatz set, advancing the search for non-Clifford gates needed for fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: Explicit Separations for One-Query Unitary Synthesis
summary: The unitary synthesis problem (Aaronson-Kuperberg, CCC 2007) asks whether every $n$-qubit unitary $U$ is computable by efficient quantum circuits relative to some classical oracle $f = f_U$ depending on $U$. Recently, Lombardi-Ma-Wright (STOC 2024) proved that Haar-random unitaries cannot be efficiently synthesized by algorithms that make 1 query (or poly$(n)$ parallel queries) to an arbitrary classical oracle. In this work, we prove several results about the hardness (and easiness!) of variants of unitary synthesis. Our results include: (1) 1-query vs. 2-query unitary synthesis: we prove 1-query lower bounds for synthesizing random permutation unitaries $P\lvert x\rangle = \lvert π(x)\rangle$, as well as random alternating-basis phase unitaries $F_2 \cdot H^{\otimes n} \cdot F_1$. This gives 1-query lower bounds for "explicit" families of unitaries that have efficient (even 2-query) synthesis algorithms. (2) Upper bound for complex phase unitaries: we also consider complex phase unitaries $\lvert x\rangle\mapsto α_x \lvert x\rangle$, which have a clean 2-query synthesis algorithm with no obvious 1-query algorithm. In this case, we prove an upper bound: there are 1-query algorithms (relative to binary phase oracles) that constant-approximate these unitaries in diamond distance. In order to prove our lower bounds, we introduce and analyze two new cryptographic games: the oracle state search game and the oracle Choi state game. Compared to prior work, our framework is mathematically simple, more flexible in what it can prove, and more accurately captures the hardness of synthesizing unitaries that are not "fully random". Finally, we also use the search game to prove a new hardness-of-approximation result for quantum programs (synthesizing unitaries relative to quantum advice) for phase unitaries, giving a sharper separation between 1-query unitary synthesis and quantum programs.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the unitary synthesis problem, proving that certain families of unitaries (random permutation unitaries, alternating-basis phase unitaries) cannot be synthesized with 1 query to a classical oracle but can be with 2 queries, while complex phase unitaries admit 1-query approximation algorithms. The authors introduce two new cryptographic games (oracle state search game and oracle Choi state game) to prove these lower bounds, and also show a hardness-of-approximation result for quantum programs.
AI.motivation: To understand the query complexity landscape of unitary synthesis—specifically, to characterize which unitaries can be efficiently synthesized with limited queries to classical oracles, and to develop more flexible tools for proving lower bounds that work beyond "fully random" Haar-random unitaries.
AI.method: The paper introduces two new cryptographic games: (1) the oracle state search game and (2) the oracle Choi state game. These games provide a mathematically simple and flexible framework for proving lower bounds on unitary synthesis. The authors analyze specific unitary families: random permutation unitaries, random alternating-basis phase unitaries, and complex phase unitaries, and prove both lower bounds (1-query hardness) and upper bounds (1-query approximation algorithms).
AI.result: (1) 1-query lower bounds for synthesizing random permutation unitaries and random alternating-basis phase unitaries, despite these families having efficient 2-query algorithms. (2) An upper bound showing that complex phase unitaries can be constant-approximated in diamond distance by 1-query algorithms relative to binary phase oracles. (3) A new hardness-of-approximation result for quantum programs for phase unitaries, showing a sharper separation between 1-query unitary synthesis and quantum programs.
AI.conclusion: The framework of oracle state search game and oracle Choi state game is more flexible and mathematically simpler than prior approaches, enabling lower bounds for "explicit" unitary families (not just Haar-random). The results reveal nuanced query complexity separations (1 vs 2 queries) and trade-offs between exact synthesis and approximate synthesis in unitary synthesis problems.

title: Feedback stabilization of multi-qubit Hamiltonian parameters enabled by single-shot measurement-based sequential Monte Carlo
summary: Fast measurement, signal processing, and accurate estimation of Hamiltonian parameters are essential for feedback control in quantum-classical interface circuitry. However, existing frequentist and Bayesian inference methods typically require a large number of measurements to achieve the accuracy needed to mitigate qubit decoherence. Consequently, feedback control of semiconductor qubits has largely been limited to single-qubit frequency stabilization, whereas two-qubit parameter stabilization remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we demonstrate a real-time feedback framework based on sequential Monte Carlo estimation using one bit of data from a single-shot measurement. Using a four-qubit semiconductor quantum dot device, we rapidly estimate individual qubit frequencies, yielding an approximately twofold increase in coherence time compared with a conventional Bayesian strategy. Moreover, sequential two-qubit parameter estimation using two bits of data enables stabilization of qubit-qubit coupling, allowing both quasi-static frequency drift and exchange-interaction noise to be estimated and suppressed. By shortening the time required for precise parameter estimation, these results demonstrate the importance of the synergistic development of classical and quantum electronics for building robust and scalable quantum technologies in fluctuating environments.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a real-time feedback framework using sequential Monte Carlo estimation with single-bit data from single-shot measurements. Applied to a four-qubit semiconductor quantum dot device, this method achieves ~2x improvement in coherence time over conventional Bayesian strategies and enables stabilization of qubit-qubit coupling by estimating and suppressing both frequency drift and exchange-interaction noise.
AI.motivation: Existing frequentist and Bayesian inference methods require a large number of measurements to achieve the accuracy needed for mitigating qubit decoherence, limiting feedback control of semiconductor qubits to single-qubit frequency stabilization while two-qubit parameter stabilization remains experimentally unexplored.
AI.method: Sequential Monte Carlo estimation using one bit of data from a single-shot measurement, applied in a real-time feedback framework on a four-qubit semiconductor quantum dot device.
AI.result: Approximately twofold increase in coherence time compared with a conventional Bayesian strategy for individual qubit frequencies; successful two-qubit parameter estimation using two bits of data enabling stabilization of qubit-qubit coupling; suppression of both quasi-static frequency drift and exchange-interaction noise.
AI.conclusion: Shortening the time required for precise parameter estimation through synergistic development of classical and quantum electronics is critical for building robust and scalable quantum technologies in fluctuating environments.

title: Quantum random number generation using spatial quantum noise of light
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures; Accepted for publication in Applied Physics Letters
summary: Generating high-speed, verifiable random numbers is a fundamental requirement for cryptography, large-scale stochastic simulations, and secure quantum communication. Here, we present a robust quantum random number generator that utilizes the spatial distribution of quantum fluctuations captured by an electron-multiplying charge-coupled device operated in high-speed kinetic mode. Through rigorous detector calibration and shot-noise analysis, we characterize the spatial quantum noise obtained from the spatial intensity fluctuations of the coherent states of light. Such quantum noise serves as a high-entropy source, enabling an instantaneous random bit generation rate of 5.92 Gbps without algorithmic randomness extraction in the present configuration. The sustained output rate is, however, limited to 7.5 Mbps by the bandwidth of the serial electronic readout. The generated sequences successfully pass the NIST SP 800-22 and Marsaglia Diehard statistical test suites, confirming the high quality and unpredictability of the entropy source.

AI.tldr: A quantum random number generator achieves 5.92 Gbps instantaneous bit rate using spatial quantum fluctuations from coherent light imaged on an EMCCD in kinetic mode, bypassing algorithmic extraction, with generated sequences passing NIST and Diehard tests.
AI.motivation: High-speed, verifiable random numbers are essential for cryptography, stochastic simulations, and quantum communication, motivating the development of a robust QRNG leveraging spatial quantum noise.
AI.method: Spatial intensity fluctuations of coherent states of light are captured by an EMCCD in high-speed kinetic mode; detector calibration and shot-noise analysis characterize the quantum noise as a high-entropy source without algorithmic randomness extraction.
AI.result: Instantaneous random bit generation rate of 5.92 Gbps; sustained output rate limited to 7.5 Mbps by serial readout bandwidth; sequences pass NIST SP 800-22 and Marsaglia Diehard tests.
AI.conclusion: Spatial quantum noise from coherent states provides a high-entropy source for robust, verifiable QRNG with high instantaneous rates, though sustained throughput is constrained by electronic readout limitations.

title: Converting Quantum Sensing Noise into Erasures
summary: Erasures are more favorable for quantum sensing than unflagged errors such as Pauli errors. However, realistic sensing noise does not usually appear as erasures; it often acts within the same sensing Hilbert space as the signal, making it difficult to identify and mitigate. For such noise, we establish a noise-model-agnostic necessary and sufficient condition for erasure conversion, identifying the noise components that can be converted into erasures and removed without damaging the signal. For components satisfying the condition, conversion can be realized by a passive dimension-lifted scheme requiring neither detailed noise knowledge nor active control. Theoretically, the protocol remains effective over a broad range of noise strengths and approaches the corresponding precision limit. Experimentally, in single-photon phase sensing, we recover standard-quantum-limit precision in a Pauli-noise channel with erasure-convertible weight 0.5, using orbital angular momentum as the ancilla. These results provide a practical route to robust quantum sensing under realistic noise.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a noise-model-agnostic condition for converting realistic sensing noise into erasures, enabling robust quantum sensing without detailed noise knowledge. The protocol is demonstrated experimentally in single-photon phase sensing, recovering standard-quantum-limit precision under Pauli noise.
AI.motivation: Realistic quantum sensing noise (e.g., Pauli errors) acts within the same Hilbert space as the signal, making it difficult to identify and mitigate. Erasures are more favorable for sensing than unflagged errors, but realistic noise does not naturally appear as erasures.
AI.method: The authors derive a noise-model-agnostic necessary and sufficient condition for erasure conversion, identifying which noise components can be converted into erasures without damaging the signal. They propose a passive dimension-lifted scheme requiring neither detailed noise knowledge nor active control. Experimental validation uses single-photon phase sensing with orbital angular momentum as an ancilla.
AI.result: The protocol remains effective over a broad range of noise strengths and approaches the corresponding precision limit. In experiment, they recover standard-quantum-limit precision in a Pauli-noise channel with erasure-convertible weight 0.5.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical, noise-model-agnostic route to robust quantum sensing under realistic noise, demonstrating that erasure conversion can be achieved passively without detailed noise knowledge or active control.

title: QKD-Integrated Quantum Noise Stream Cipher: An Overview
summary: Quantum Noise Stream Cipher (QNSC) has emerged as a physical-layer encryption technique that exploits quantum noise and non-orthogonal coherent-state modulation to secure optical communication. However, the security of QNSC relies exceedingly on the secrecy and freshness of its seed key. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), on the other hand, provides information-theoretically secure key exchange rooted in the laws of quantum mechanics. The convergence of these two paradigms, i.e., integrated QKD-QNSC architectures, offers a compelling solution to each of their limitations. In such integrated systems, QKD continuously supplies and refreshes the secret seed key that governs QNSC modulation. Thus, governing a unified security framework that couples provably secure key establishment with high-speed quantum-enhanced physical-layer encryption. This work presents a comprehensive review of QNSC systems, examining their operating principles, security models under various attacks, and their integration with QKD systems. We analyze the security interplay between the key generation and encryption layers and survey experimental demonstrations and architectural progress toward practical deployment. Furthermore, we identify the open challenges and future research directions that must be addressed to realize fully integrated, quantum-secured optical communication networks at a practical scale.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews Quantum Noise Stream Cipher (QNSC) systems integrated with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), examining their operating principles, security models, experimental demonstrations, and open challenges for practical quantum-secured optical networks.
AI.motivation: QNSC's security depends on the secrecy and freshness of its seed key, while QKD provides information-theoretically secure key exchange. Integrating these two paradigms overcomes each technique's individual limitations, offering a unified security framework for high-speed quantum-enhanced physical-layer encryption.
AI.method: A comprehensive review approach covering QNSC operating principles, security models under various attacks, QKD integration architectures, security interplay between key generation and encryption layers, and experimental demonstrations.
AI.result: Survey of security interplay between QKD key generation and QNSC encryption layers, along with experimental demonstrations and architectural progress toward practical deployment of integrated QKD-QNSC systems.
AI.conclusion: Identifies open challenges and future research directions necessary for realizing fully integrated, quantum-secured optical communication networks at a practical scale.

title: Quantum model reduction based on Oja's flow
summary: We propose a novel approach to numerically derive approximate reduced dynamical models for Markovian quantum open systems without perturbative iterations, projecting the evolution to the subspace associated to their slowest degrees of freedom. The two algorithms we develop are based on Oja's continuous-time principal component flow: the first returns the optimal reduction to the slowest decaying operator-subspace, and is extended to time-dependent dynamics, while the second one is designed to reduce the dynamics on a subspace of the system's Hilbert space, and thus preserve conditional complete positivity. The methods represent a non-perturbative alternative to well-established Adiabatic Elimination (AE) methods, and the second can be used to find noise-protected subspace codes for quantum information processing. Both are tested on a paradigmatic central spin model.

AI.tldr: The paper presents two non-perturbative algorithms based on Oja's continuous-time principal component flow to derive reduced dynamical models for Markovian quantum open systems by projecting onto slowest degrees of freedom, offering alternatives to Adiabatic Elimination methods and enabling noise-protected subspace code discovery.
AI.motivation: To develop non-perturbative methods for deriving approximate reduced dynamical models of Markovian quantum open systems that project onto the slowest degrees of freedom, overcoming limitations of perturbative Adiabatic Elimination approaches.
AI.method: Two algorithms based on Oja's continuous-time principal component flow: (1) optimal reduction to the slowest decaying operator-subspace with extension to time-dependent dynamics; (2) reduction on a subspace of the system's Hilbert space preserving conditional complete positivity.
AI.result: Both methods are tested on a paradigmatic central spin model, demonstrating their effectiveness as non-perturbative alternatives to traditional Adiabatic Elimination methods.
AI.conclusion: The second algorithm can be used to find noise-protected subspace codes for quantum information processing, and both methods provide a non-perturbative framework for dimension reduction of quantum open systems.

title: Relational Quantum Causal Processes: Exact Models, Continuum Limits, and the Boundary of Emergent Gravity
summary: Relational quantum causal processes formulate finite operational contexts as normal positive functionals on local completely positive maps. Response differences generate an influence algebra, and its central projections define jointly readable Boolean events. We develop this starting point through a sequence of exact and controlled models. Fresh-environment unitary collision circuits produce dephasing-exchange kinetics with an exact charge-center fixed algebra, a uniform finite-step limit at fixed response order, and graph-controlled metastable Markov dynamics. An absorbing-state model exhibits a sharp transition between non-Abelian quantum memory and Boolean records. A reversal-covariant defect dynamics generates a locally finite partial order on a restricted graph family without assuming a Lyapunov time. Conditional on a certified order, a positive additive record measure, compactness, and identifiability, we prove subsequential convergence to a Lorentzian metric-measure space, finite reconstruction bounds, and uniqueness of admissible smooth limits. Complementary finite regulators provide controlled tests of modular-to-boost response, null tomography, same-update variational identities, induced quadratic gravity, and compatible common-refinement limits. These results are exact or controlled within their stated models, but they do not yet constitute a single background-independent microscopic law that jointly generates adjacency, time, volume normalization, dimension, signature, nonlinear Einstein constraints, and quantum matter. We therefore present RQCP-QG as a theorem-indexed framework that separates established mechanisms, conditional compositions, and open assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper develops Relational Quantum Causal Processes (RQCP) through exact models including dephasing-exchange kinetics, absorbing-state transitions, and reversal-covariant defect dynamics, proving subsequential convergence to Lorentzian metric-measure space under certain conditions, while presenting the framework as theorem-indexed with established mechanisms and open assumptions rather than a complete quantum gravity theory.
AI.motivation: To develop relational quantum causal processes as a framework for understanding quantum causal structures, starting from finite operational contexts and building toward potential quantum gravity applications, while being transparent about what is proven and what remains assumed.
AI.method: Uses normal positive functionals on local completely positive maps to define influence algebras and jointly readable Boolean events. Develops exact and controlled models: fresh-environment unitary collision circuits, absorbing-state models, reversal-covariant defect dynamics, and finite regulators. Proves subsequential convergence using conditions of certified order, positive additive record measure, compactness, and identifiability.
AI.result: Demonstrates dephasing-exchange kinetics with exact charge-center fixed algebra and graph-controlled metastable Markov dynamics. Shows sharp transition between non-Abelian quantum memory and Boolean records. Proves subsequential convergence to Lorentzian metric-measure space, finite reconstruction bounds, and uniqueness of admissible smooth limits under specified conditions. Finite regulators provide controlled tests of modular-to-boost response, null tomography, and induced quadratic gravity.
AI.conclusion: The results do not yet constitute a complete background-independent microscopic law generating all required features (adjacency, time, dimension, signature, Einstein constraints, quantum matter). RQCP-QG is presented as a theorem-indexed framework separating established mechanisms, conditional compositions, and open assumptions.

title: Microscopic study of topological phase transitions: Percolation point of view
comment: 21 pages, 19 main figures and 2 figures in Appendix
summary:
We investigate microscopic mechanisms underlying decoherence-induced transitions between topologically ordered states. As a first case study, we analyze the color code using topological entanglement negativity (TEN) and a disorder parameter associated with 1-form symmetry. We interpret these quantities as first- and zeroth-dimensional simplicial homological objects, respectively, and show that the transition can be understood in terms of decoherence percolation. To resolve its local structure, we introduce quasi-local TEN (QLTEN), which visualizes the spatial distribution of local topological properties and the growth of decohered regions.
  We further introduce explosive percolation (EP), corresponding here to biased decoherence that suppresses the formation of large decohered clusters. As a second case study, we consider the toric code on a triangular lattice under external-field-type decoherence. Numerical results show that QLTEN faithfully captures the emergence of Higgs regions and the survival of logical qubits. Although global TEN, QLTEN clusters, and string operators are strongly correlated in both models, the color code and toric code respond differently to EP patterns. This difference indicates that a universal microscopic description of decoherence-induced topological phase transitions remains challenging even for closely related systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies decoherence-induced topological phase transitions in the color code and toric code using topological entanglement negativity (TEN), quasi-local TEN (QLTEN), and explosive percolation (EP). The color code analysis uses simplicial homological interpretations and decoherence percolation, while the toric code on a triangular lattice reveals Higgs region formation and logical qubit survival. Both models show strong correlation among TEN, QLTEN clusters, and string operators, but respond differently to EP patterns, suggesting universal microscopic descriptions remain challenging.
AI.motivation: To understand microscopic mechanisms underlying decoherence-induced transitions between topologically ordered states, particularly how local topological properties evolve under biased decoherence.
AI.method: The authors use topological entanglement negativity (TEN) interpreted as first-dimensional simplicial homology, a disorder parameter for 1-form symmetry (zeroth-dimensional homology), quasi-local TEN (QLTEN) for spatial visualization, and explosive percolation (EP) as biased decoherence. Two models are studied: the color code and the toric code on a triangular lattice.
AI.result: QLTEN faithfully captures Higgs region emergence and logical qubit survival in the toric code. Global TEN, QLTEN clusters, and string operators are strongly correlated in both models. However, the color code and toric code respond differently to EP patterns.
AI.conclusion: A universal microscopic description of decoherence-induced topological phase transitions remains challenging even for closely related systems like the color code and toric code, due to their different responses to biased decoherence patterns.

title: Generative AI Beyond Tokens: Quantum Resource Consumption of IQP Circuits
summary: Quantum generative modelling casts sampling as a generative task: a parametrised quantum circuit is trained such that sampling reproduces a target probability distribution. Instantaneous Quantum Polynomial-time (IQP) circuits combine structural simplicity with complexity-theoretic evidence for quantum advantage. Yet their practical value depends not only on expressivity, but on how efficiently they consume genuinely quantum resources. We study this question through the lens of magic, or non-stabiliserness, as a resource for quantum generative modelling. We show that established fidelity- and geodesic-based notions of computational progress in a projective Hilbert space are ill-suited to generative models, since operational performance is determined by output probability distributions rather than quantum states themselves. We evaluate magic-consumption directly on the probability simplex, using changes in Jensen-Shannon divergence to quantify progress. Applying this framework to trained random γ-sparse IQP circuits shows signatures of efficient magic use, with the dominant contribution arising from two-qubit gates. As IQP circuits produce remarkably low intermediate magic relative to phase-randomised states with the same sampling distributions, this renders IQP-based quantum generative models as promising candidates for resource-efficient demonstrations of quantum advantage on early fault-tolerant architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how IQP circuits consume magic (non-stabiliserness) as a resource for quantum generative modelling, proposing a probability-simplex-based framework using Jensen-Shannon divergence to evaluate magic efficiency, and finding that IQP-based generative models use magic efficiently with dominant contributions from two-qubit gates, making them promising for early fault-tolerant quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Existing fidelity- and geodesic-based notions of computational progress in projective Hilbert space are ill-suited for generative models, as operational performance is determined by output probability distributions rather than quantum states themselves. The practical value of IQP circuits for generative modelling depends on how efficiently they consume genuinely quantum resources (magic).
AI.method: The authors evaluate magic-consumption directly on the probability simplex using changes in Jensen-Shannon divergence to quantify progress, and apply this framework to trained random γ-sparse IQP circuits.
AI.result: Trained random γ-sparse IQP circuits show signatures of efficient magic use, with the dominant contribution arising from two-qubit gates. IQP circuits produce remarkably low intermediate magic relative to phase-randomised states with the same sampling distributions.
AI.conclusion: IQP-based quantum generative models are promising candidates for resource-efficient demonstrations of quantum advantage on early fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Coherent electric field manipulation of nuclear spin qudit
summary: Spins in condensed matter, especially well-isolated nuclear spins, offer attractive quantum degrees of freedom for computing, sensing, and networking because of their long coherence times. The possibility of electric-field control is an important feature for practical scalable quantum technologies, but, typically, nuclear spins couple only weakly to electric fields in conventional semiconductor hosts, limiting operation efficiency. Here we show that a choice of a highly polarizable oxide host can overcome this bottleneck. In Mn2+ doped ZnO, electric-field modulation of the spin Hamiltonian is amplified by hyperfine-coupled electron spins, and offers efficient electric-field manipulation of an I = 5/2 nuclear spin qudit, in a manner analogous to the hyperfine enhancement of conventional nuclear magnetic resonance. We demonstrate both resonant and non-resonant coherent manipulation using a single uniaxial electric field applied along the crystalline c-axis, the polarization axis of ZnO. This approach allows universal single-qudit gate operations with efficiencies comparable to or exceeding those of conventional magnetic-field driving. These results support the deployment of doped oxides as active host materials for electrically controllable spin qubits, highlighting the importance of materials design in developing scalable quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that electric-field control of nuclear spin qudits can be achieved efficiently by using a highly polarizable oxide host (MnO2-doped ZnO), where hyperfine coupling to electron spins amplifies electric-field modulation. This enables resonant and non-resonant coherent manipulation of an I=5/2 nuclear spin qudit with performance comparable to magnetic driving, supporting the use of doped oxides for scalable quantum technologies.
AI.motivation: Nuclear spins have long coherence times and are attractive for quantum technologies, but they couple weakly to electric fields in conventional semiconductors, limiting scalability. The authors aim to overcome this bottleneck by using a highly polarizable oxide host material.
AI.method: The authors use Mn2+-doped ZnO as the host material, where hyperfine coupling between the Mn2+ electron spin and the I=5/2 nuclear spin amplifies electric-field modulation of the spin Hamiltonian. They apply a uniaxial electric field along the crystalline c-axis (polarization axis of ZnO) and demonstrate both resonant and non-resonant coherent manipulation of the nuclear spin qudit.
AI.result: Efficient electric-field manipulation of an I=5/2 nuclear spin qudit is achieved, with universal single-qudit gate operations showing efficiencies comparable to or exceeding conventional magnetic-field driving.
AI.conclusion: The results support the deployment of doped oxides as active host materials for electrically controllable spin qubits, highlighting the importance of materials design in developing scalable quantum technologies.

title: High-fidelity multiqubit gates with Rydberg atoms via level-crossing-free Rapid adiabatic passage
summary: We propose a rapid adiabatic passage (RAP) scheme based on level-crossing-free pulses for deterministic generation of multiqubit entangled states in Rydberg atom systems. Unlike conventional RAP protocols that rely on level crossings, our approach uses an antisymmetric Rabi frequency and an even-symmetric detuning, enabling robust population transfer without passing through any level crossing. By exploiting the Rydberg blockade effect, the protocol prepares entangled states directly from an initial product state. Specifically, two sequential RAP pulses separated by a pi_g pulse generate two-qubit Bell states, three-qubit W states, four-qubit GHZ states, and six-qubit honeycomb W states. Numerical simulations show that the fidelities exceed 0.9997 for the Bell and three-qubit W states, reach 0.997 for the four-qubit GHZ state, and surpass 0.9995 for the six-qubit honeycomb W state. The scheme demonstrates excellent robustness against pulse parameter fluctuations, with fidelities remaining above 0.99 under +/-5% parameter variations. This work provides a simple, efficient, and robust method for entangled-state preparation in neutral-atom quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: A RAP scheme using level-crossing-free pulses is proposed for deterministic generation of multiqubit entangled states (Bell, W, GHZ, honeycomb W) in Rydberg atom systems, achieving fidelities >0.9997 for Bell/3-qubit W, 0.997 for 4-qubit GHZ, and >0.9995 for 6-qubit honeycomb W, with robust performance under ±5% parameter variations.
AI.motivation: To develop a simple, efficient, and robust method for deterministic generation of multiqubit entangled states in Rydberg atom systems that avoids the complexity and fragility of conventional RAP protocols relying on level crossings.
AI.method: The scheme employs an antisymmetric Rabi frequency and even-symmetric detuning to achieve robust population transfer without level crossings. Sequential RAP pulses separated by a π_g pulse, combined with the Rydberg blockade effect, directly prepare entangled states from initial product states.
AI.result: Fidelities exceed 0.9997 for Bell and three-qubit W states, 0.997 for four-qubit GHZ states, and surpass 0.9995 for six-qubit honeycomb W states. Fidelities remain above 0.99 under ±5% parameter variations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed level-crossing-free RAP scheme offers a simple, efficient, and robust approach for entangled-state preparation in neutral-atom quantum information processing.

title: Label and Recover Coherent Errors: Randomized Compiling Does Not Destroy Coherent-Error Information
summary: Randomized compiling (RC) is the standard technique for converting coherent (systematic) gate errors into stochastic noise. The prevailing view is that the twirl destroys coherent-error information. An exact Fisher-information conservation law shows the opposite: the coherent-error information RC removes from the averaged output is preserved in full in the twirl labels -- the per-shot random gate choices that standard RC discards. Retaining the labels and forming a label-outcome correlation recovers the coherent error parameters at the quantum Fisher-information limit, unbiased under all standard incoherent channels, at zero additional circuit cost. Two theorems are proved, the conservation law is verified to machine precision across 12 circuit families, and recovery is confirmed on a 127-qubit IBM Quantum processor (ibm_marrakesh). The labeled estimator recovers injected coherent phases to within 0.0063 rad of the true value across all depths tested, while the standard marginal estimator returns near-zero signal at every depth.

AI.tldr: Randomized compiling does not destroy coherent error information; it is preserved in twirl labels. Using label-outcome correlations recovers coherent error parameters at the quantum Fisher-information limit with zero extra circuit cost, verified on a 127-qubit quantum processor.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing view that randomized compiling destroys coherent-error information, and to demonstrate that this information is preserved in twirl labels and can be recovered without additional circuit cost.
AI.method: Derives a Fisher-information conservation law showing coherent-error information is transferred to twirl labels. Proves two theorems, verifies the conservation law across 12 circuit families to machine precision, and validates recovery on a 127-qubit IBM Quantum processor (ibm_marrakesh) by forming label-outcome correlations.
AI.result: Labeled estimator recovers injected coherent phases to within 0.0063 rad of true value across all depths; standard marginal estimator returns near-zero signal at every depth. Verification to machine precision across 12 circuit families.
AI.conclusion: Coherent error information is not destroyed but preserved in twirl labels during randomized compiling, enabling unbiased recovery at the quantum Fisher-information limit with zero added circuit cost.

title: PhD thesis: Modes, States, and Symmetries in quantum Optics for quantum Information and Metrology
comment: 508 pages, 56 figures, 6 tables. Please also cite the relevant journal articles when citing the thesis
summary: This thesis explores the role of modes, states, and symmetries in quantum optics, within the context of quantum information and quantum metrology. It proposes a unified framework to analyze how the modal structure of photonic fields, the statistical nature of states, and their symmetry properties determine the physical resources that can be exploited for quantum information processing and quantum parameter estimation. A first line of investigation develops a description of time-frequency degrees of freedom as continuous quantum variables, highlighting their richness for encoding and manipulating information. A second axis studies entanglement and collective variables, clarifying the link between physical resources and metrological gains, particularly in reaching ultimate precision limits. Interferometric scenarios of the Hong-Ou-Mandel type are then analyzed, and a general formalism centered on the notion of symmetry is developed. This framework enables the analysis of a broad range of situations and leads to several generalizations. Finally, the thesis examines the symmetries imposed by optical superselection rules and their consequences for the structure of quantum states and their operational performance, with the aim of providing a deeper understanding of the foundations of quantum optics.

AI.tldr: This thesis develops a unified framework analyzing modes, states, and symmetries in quantum optics to understand how these features determine physical resources for quantum information processing and quantum metrology, covering time-frequency degrees of freedom, entanglement, collective variables, Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry, and optical superselection rules.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified understanding of how the modal structure, statistical nature, and symmetry properties of photonic fields determine the physical resources exploitable for quantum information processing and quantum parameter estimation.
AI.method: The thesis develops a unified theoretical framework across three axes: (1) describing time-frequency degrees of freedom as continuous quantum variables; (2) studying entanglement and collective variables linking physical resources to metrological gains; (3) developing a general formalism centered on symmetry for analyzing Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry and its generalizations, including the examination of optical superselection rules.
AI.result: A general symmetry-based formalism is developed that enables analysis of a broad range of interferometric scenarios, clarifies the link between physical resources and ultimate precision limits in metrology, and reveals how optical superselection rules constrain the structure of quantum states and their operational performance.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a deeper understanding of the foundations of quantum optics by unifying the analysis of modes, states, and symmetries, with implications for quantum information processing and quantum metrology.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical end-to-end pipeline for solving MILPs: a vehicle routing case study
summary: We demonstrate an end-to-end hybrid quantum-classical optimisation framework based on Benders decomposition, capable of solving mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problems. The framework builds on a previously presented hybrid quantum-classical end-to-end pipeline based on Multiple Cuts via Multiple Solutions (MCMS) Benders decomposition where the cut selection step was performed on quantum annealing hardware. We extend this with gate-based QAOA implementations for both tensor network emulators and superconducting quantum hardware. The Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) is used as a representative case study and we run the pipeline end-to-end on 10 permutations of a standardised benchmarking instance (20 customers and 4 vehicles from QOptLib) with a classical solver performing the cut selection step. We find that for our instances, only a small fraction of the compute in classical MCMS Benders decomposition is spent on the cut selection step. For a full hybrid end-to-end assessment, we run the pipeline for a toy problem with MPS-JuliQAOA, a powerful tensor network emulator, to execute QAOA. Here, the majority of the time is spent on the cut selection step, deeming quantum advantage of this framework unlikely at problems of this size. This highlights the need for more large-scale benchmarking research when more powerful (QPU) QUBO solvers are available.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical optimization framework based on Benders decomposition for solving MILP problems, extending prior work with gate-based QAOA implementations. Using VRP as a case study, they find that only a small fraction of classical compute time is spent on cut selection, while in the hybrid quantum approach, cut selection dominates runtime, making quantum advantage unlikely at the tested problem sizes.
AI.motivation: To extend hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks based on Benders decomposition by incorporating gate-based QAOA implementations, and to assess whether quantum advantage is achievable in practice for MILP problems like VRP.
AI.method: Extended a previously proposed MCMS Benders decomposition pipeline by adding gate-based QAOA implementations using both tensor network emulators (MPS-JuliQAOA) and superconducting quantum hardware. Evaluated on 10 permutations of a standardized 20-customer, 4-vehicle VRP instance (QOptLib). Classical solver performed cut selection in the main benchmark; toy problem used for full hybrid end-to-end assessment.
AI.result: In classical MCMS Benders decomposition, only a small fraction of compute time is spent on cut selection. In the full hybrid quantum pipeline, the majority of time is spent on cut selection, making quantum advantage unlikely at this problem size.
AI.conclusion: Quantum advantage for this hybrid Benders decomposition framework is unlikely at the tested problem sizes; more large-scale benchmarking is needed when more powerful QUBO solvers become available.

title: Enforcing IID structure on time-bin encoded QKD protocols via coarse-graining
summary: Many security proofs for quantum key distribution (QKD) require Bob's measurement to have a tensor-product structure across protocol rounds, with some techniques requiring the stronger independent-and-identically-distributed (IID) condition. Time-bin encoded protocols often rely on interferometers whose detector outcomes depend on the interference between optical modes from neighbouring rounds, obstructing the direct application of such proofs. We show that classical post-processing of Bob's measurement data --- specifically, discarding the outcomes of detectors sensitive to inter-round coherence --- is sufficient to recover a product measurement positive operator-valued measure (POVM) (which is IID when the same single-round setup is used in every round). Applied to the Mach-Zehnder interferometer and the IID variant of the COW detection setup, this removes the need for the additional vacuum pulse introduced in prior analyses to establish tensor product structure of the measurement POVM, recovering better key rates without placing any restriction on Eve's attack.

AI.tldr: Time-bin encoded QKD protocols using interferometers break the tensor-product structure needed for security proofs. This paper shows that discarding detector outcomes sensitive to inter-round coherence recovers a product measurement POVM (IID if the setup is consistent per round), eliminating the need for vacuum pulses used in prior analyses and achieving better key rates under general attacks.
AI.motivation: Time-bin encoded QKD protocols using interferometers produce detector outcomes that depend on interference between optical modes from neighboring rounds, breaking the tensor-product structure (and stronger IID condition) required by many QKD security proofs, thus obstructing their direct application.
AI.method: Classical post-processing of Bob's measurement data: specifically, discarding the outcomes of detectors that are sensitive to inter-round coherence, thereby recovering a product measurement POVM (which is IID when the same single-round setup is used every round). Applied to Mach-Zehnder interferometer and the IID variant of the COW detection setup.
AI.result: Removes the need for the additional vacuum pulse introduced in prior analyses to establish tensor-product structure; recovers better key rates without placing any restriction on Eve's attack.
AI.conclusion: A simple classical post-processing step (discarding coherence-sensitive detector outcomes) suffices to restore the tensor-product and IID structure required for QKD security proofs in time-bin encoded protocols, yielding improved key rates under unrestricted attacks.

title: Enhancing the security of coherent one-way quantum key distribution using CHSH correlations
summary: The coherent one-way (COW) protocol is a quantum key distribution scheme that has attracted significant attention, leading to the development and commercialization of practical implementations. Despite this progress, the security of the COW protocol has remained a fundamental challenge since its introduction. Numerous studies have investigated its security, and several security proofs have been proposed over the years. More recently, a number of works have questioned the security of this protocol. In particular, one of the latest studies introduced an attack that severely limits the security of COW-QKD and reported a maximum secure distance of less than 20km. In this work, we introduce minimal alteration to the COW protocol that can enhance its security. Specifically, instead of monitoring the coherence between successive pulses, we propose to monitor quantum correlations through the violation of Bell inequalities. This approach enables the detection of a broader class of potential attacks. Our simulation results indicate that, by employing this method, the maximum secure distance of the protocol can be extended to approximately 259km.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes modifying the COW QKD protocol to use Bell inequality violation instead of coherence monitoring, extending the maximum secure distance from less than 20km to approximately 259km.
AI.motivation: Despite commercialization of the COW protocol, its security has remained a fundamental challenge, with recent attacks limiting its secure distance to less than 20km.
AI.method: Instead of monitoring coherence between successive pulses (as in the original COW protocol), the authors propose monitoring quantum correlations through the violation of Bell inequalities, requiring only minimal alteration to the original protocol.
AI.result: Simulation results show the maximum secure distance can be extended from less than 20km to approximately 259km using the proposed Bell inequality-based monitoring approach.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring Bell inequality violations instead of coherence significantly enhances the security of the COW protocol, enabling detection of a broader class of attacks and greatly extending the secure transmission distance.

title: Analytical Series Expansion for Efficient Gradient Evaluation in Multi-Qubit Optimal Control
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 13 pages, 2 figures
summary: The open-loop optimization of quantum dynamics using gradient-based quantum optimal control methods involves calculating the time-ordered propagator and its gradient. In this Letter, we present a unifying framework for gradient-based quantum optimal control with respect to any general pulse parameterization by deriving the formal solution from first principles. For the case of unitary propagators, we derive a series expansion involving time-independent commutators and time-dependent coefficients, significantly reducing the number of matrix exponentials needed to compute the gradient. The expansion highlights the connection between derivatives of the propagator and operator evolution in the Heisenberg picture. The method is particularly suited for simulating optimal control tasks in quantum systems with local interactions, which is a common situation in large multi-qubit platforms. We compare the computational cost required for the series with the Gradient Optimization of Analytic conTrols (GOAT) method, and, focusing on the problem of preparation of a GHZ state, demonstrate more than an order of magnitude speedup for a qubit ladder and a chain geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unifying framework for gradient-based quantum optimal control that uses a series expansion with time-independent commutators to reduce matrix exponentials, enabling order-of-magnitude speedups for simulating optimal control in local-interaction quantum systems, demonstrated on GHZ state preparation.
AI.motivation: To develop a more computationally efficient gradient-based quantum optimal control method for open-loop optimization of quantum dynamics, particularly for large multi-qubit systems with local interactions.
AI.method: The authors derive a formal solution from first principles for gradient-based quantum optimal control with general pulse parameterization. For unitary propagators, they derive a series expansion using time-independent commutators and time-dependent coefficients, which reduces the number of required matrix exponentials for gradient computation.
AI.result: The method demonstrates more than an order of magnitude speedup compared to the GOAT method for preparing GHZ states on both qubit ladder and chain geometries.
AI.conclusion: The proposed series expansion framework connects derivatives of the propagator to operator evolution in the Heisenberg picture, and is particularly advantageous for quantum systems with local interactions, offering significant computational savings for optimal control tasks in large multi-qubit platforms.

title: Calibrated Pressure-Observable Born and Hessian Actions for Quantum-Assisted Waveform Inversion
comment: 21-page main manuscript with a 16-page supplement; 11 figures in total
summary: We construct a pressure-consistent operator-and-readout interface for Born, adjoint, and Gauss--Newton actions in constant-density acoustic full-waveform inversion (FWI) using Schrödingerised propagation. The energy variables $π=c^{-1}\partial_t u$ and $q=\nabla u$ yield an auxiliary-space Hamiltonian, while physical pressure $p=cπ$ depends explicitly on wavespeed. Its derivative $D(cπ)[c_0](δc)=c_0δπ+δc\,π_0$ combines propagated wavefield sensitivity with a direct receiver-calibration term. Duhamel and receiver-row differentiation retain both contributions in the Born map, its adjoint, and the Gauss--Newton normal action. We prove a conditional consistency estimate with a periodic second-order finite-difference specialization and give a resource model for state preparation, normalization, quadrature, and selected-output measurement. A compiled nine-qubit instance realizes structured preparation, product-formula propagation, a derivative-LCU block, and calibrated pressure-overlap measurements. Bernoulli samples from ideal-circuit probabilities drive a four-parameter hybrid inversion. A two-qubit VQLS circuit represents the normalized update direction, while normal-system assembly, line search, and model refresh remain classical. Finite differences, tangent and reverse-adjoint recurrences, autodiff JVP/VJP evaluations, and explicit Jacobians verify the discrete Born, adjoint, and normal actions. Smooth periodic refinement confirms second-order convergence, whereas omitting receiver calibration leaves an order-one Born error and substantially changes the regularized Gauss--Newton direction. All ten predeclared finite-shot runs reduce the initial model error. These results specify the physical-pressure derivative and selected-output measurements needed to connect Schrödingerised propagation to a local FWI update.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a pressure-consistent operator-and-readout interface for acoustic full-waveform inversion (FWI) using Schrödingerised propagation. It defines the physical pressure derivative, implements Born/adjoint/Gauss-Newton actions via Duhamel and receiver-row differentiation, proves consistency for a periodic second-order finite-difference scheme, and validates with a nine-qubit compiled circuit and hybrid inversion workflow. Results show second-order convergence and the critical importance of receiver calibration.
AI.motivation: To connect Schrödingerised quantum propagation to local FWI updates by constructing a physically consistent pressure operator and readout scheme that correctly captures the pressure derivative, including both wavefield sensitivity and direct receiver-calibration contributions.
AI.method: Uses energy variables π and q to form an auxiliary-space Hamiltonian; derives the physical pressure derivative D(cπ)[c₀](δc)=c₀δπ+δc π₀; applies Duhamel and receiver-row differentiation to retain both contributions in Born, adjoint, and Gauss-Newton actions; proves conditional consistency with a periodic second-order finite-difference specialization; implements a nine-qubit compiled circuit with structured state preparation, product-formula propagation, derivative LCU block, and calibrated pressure-overlap measurements; uses Bernoulli sampling and hybrid classical-quantum inversion.
AI.result: Second-order convergence in smooth periodic refinement; omitting receiver calibration leads to order-one Born error and substantially changes the regularized Gauss-Newton direction; all ten predeclared finite-shot runs reduce initial model error.
AI.conclusion: The physical-pressure derivative and selected-output measurements are specified and verified, providing a necessary interface to connect Schrödingerised propagation to a local FWI update.

title: Revival of transport reciprocity via quantum interference in asymmetric nonlinear devices
summary: Structural asymmetry combined with optical nonlinearity often leads to nonreciprocal light transport. We explore the mechanism by which 1-photon interference effects can revive reciprocity in such nonlinear models. To this end, we study correlated 2-photon scattering where an artificial atom is asymmetrically (a) side-coupled to an infinite waveguide at two spatially separated points, and (b) direct-coupled to two semi-infinite waveguides. The setup (a) gives robust reciprocal transport for the two photons. However, the setup (b) shows a transition from a nonreciprocal to a reciprocal regime by tuning the interference effect via an additional tunneling path for photons between the two waveguides.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how 1-photon interference effects can restore reciprocity in structurally asymmetric nonlinear optical systems, studying correlated 2-photon scattering in two different waveguide setups.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism by which single-photon interference effects can revive reciprocity in nonlinear optical systems where structural asymmetry combined with optical nonlinearity typically leads to nonreciprocal light transport.
AI.method: The authors study correlated 2-photon scattering in two configurations: (a) an artificial atom asymmetrically side-coupled to an infinite waveguide at two spatially separated points, and (b) an artificial atom direct-coupled to two semi-infinite waveguides, with an additional tunneling path between the waveguides to tune interference effects.
AI.result: Setup (a) exhibits robust reciprocal transport for two photons. Setup (b) demonstrates a transition from nonreciprocal to reciprocal behavior by tuning the interference effect through an additional photon tunneling path between the two waveguides.
AI.conclusion: One-photon interference effects can restore reciprocity in nonlinear systems, with the degree of reciprocity controllable via additional tunneling paths that mediate interference.

title: Optimization of C-band quantum traffic coexisting with O-band classical traffic: preliminary results
comment: Accepted manuscript for publication in IEEE MeditCom26. This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n.101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: The coexistence of quantum and classical signals in the same optical fiber is a critical challenge for the deployment of quantum networks. Indeed, selecting an optimal channel for quantum signal transmission is crucial to minimize noise arising from co-propagating classical signals. This work experimentally investigates spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS), a major source of noise in signals transmitted along the same fiber. Unlike most previous studies relying on narrow-linewidth laboratory lasers or architectures based on spatial or temporal multiplexing of quantum and classical signals, we employ commercial SFP optical transceivers and standard single-core single-mode fiber for the transmission of quantum and classical signals in the same fiber, reflecting conditions typical of deployed urban fiber infrastructures. Building on these measurements, we derive a compact and predictive model that captures the Raman scattering profile, enabling accurate estimation of SpRS noise as a function of source power, wavelength, and fiber length. A key outcome of this work is that the proposed model is independent of the specific optical source used, demonstrating its generality and robustness. The model can therefore be used for the identification of optimal C-band channels for quantum signal allocation, namely those least affected by SpRS noise generated by co-propagating O-band classical traffic. These results pave the way for a parameter-robust description of Raman scattering applicable to diverse fiber-based systems.

AI.tldr: This work experimentally investigates spontaneous Raman scattering (SpRS) noise from commercial SFP transceivers in standard single-mode fiber, develops a compact, source-independent predictive model for SpRS noise as a function of power, wavelength, and fiber length, and identifies optimal C-band channels for quantum signals co-propagating with O-band classical traffic in urban fiber infrastructures.
AI.motivation: The coexistence of quantum and classical signals in the same optical fiber is critical for deploying quantum networks, and selecting optimal quantum channels requires understanding noise from co-propagating classical signals, especially SpRS which is a major noise source.
AI.method: Experimental measurements using commercial SFP optical transceivers and standard single-core single-mode fiber (reflecting deployed urban fiber conditions), followed by derivation of a compact predictive model for Raman scattering profile that is independent of the specific optical source.
AI.result: A general, source-independent model for estimating SpRS noise as a function of source power, wavelength, and fiber length; identification of optimal C-band channels for quantum signals least affected by SpRS from co-propagating O-band classical traffic.
AI.conclusion: The proposed model provides a parameter-robust description of Raman scattering applicable to diverse fiber-based systems, paving the way for practical deployment of quantum-classical coexistence in urban fiber networks.

title: Sparse Quantum Voxel Encoding for Readout-Efficient Molecular Geometry Reconstruction on NISQ Devices
summary: We propose a sparse computational-basis encoding of voxelized molecular geometries that converts molecular reconstruction from full-state tomography into support recovery by computational-basis sampling. To realize the encoding scheme, the molecular space is discretized into a 3D grid, and each atom's position and chemical species is mapped to a single computational basis state. This discretization introduces spatial quantization at the voxel-resolution scale. The molecule is then encoded as an equal superposition over this sparse set of occupied states, where we assume that a suitable state preparation method exists. In contrast to full state tomography, which requires on the order of $\mathcal{O}(3^n \times 10^{2\text{--}3})$ measurement shots, where $n$ is the number of qubits, our proposed encoding scheme reduces to a coupon-collector sampling problem in the computational basis. Complete recovery of an $A$-atom molecule requires $\mathcal{O}(A\log A)$ shots on noise-free hardware. On noisy hardware, the required number of shots increases. We demonstrate the method on the 156-qubit IBM Kingston device using 8-qubit circuits to reconstruct the discretized geometry of a 10-atom ethylamine molecule with high mean reconstruction recall using only $\mathcal{O}(10^2)$ shots despite substantial hardware noise. These results demonstrate that our proposed encoding scheme is a practical, readout-efficient representation for molecular geometries on near-term devices.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a sparse computational-basis encoding of voxelized molecular geometries, converting molecular reconstruction into a coupon-collector sampling problem, requiring O(A log A) shots (vs. O(3^n×10^{2-3}) for full tomography), demonstrated on a 156-qubit IBM device reconstructing a 10-atom ethylamine molecule with O(10^2) shots.
AI.motivation: Full-state tomography for molecular reconstruction requires an impractical number of measurement shots (O(3^n×10^{2-3})). The authors seek a more readout-efficient representation for molecular geometries on near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: Discretize molecular space into a 3D voxel grid; map each atom's position and chemical species to a single computational basis state; encode the molecule as an equal superposition over the sparse set of occupied states; reconstruction reduces to support recovery via computational-basis sampling (coupon-collector problem).
AI.result: On noise-free hardware, O(A log A) shots suffice. On the 156-qubit IBM Kingston device with 8-qubit circuits, a 10-atom ethylamine molecule was reconstructed with high mean recall using only O(10^2) shots despite substantial hardware noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed sparse encoding scheme is a practical and readout-efficient representation for molecular geometries on near-term quantum devices.

title: Two-photon interference from as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots under detuned excitation
summary: In this study, we investigate as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots emitting in the third telecommunication window under detuned quasi-resonant excitation. A large excitation-emission detuning of 32 meV enables efficient suppression of scattered laser light while retaining several advantages of near-resonant excitation. The single-photon nature of the emission is confirmed by a Hanbury Brown and Twiss experiment, yielding a raw second-order autocorrelation value of $g_{\mathrm{raw}}^{(2)}(0)=0.076(6)$. Hong-Ou-Mandel measurement is used to determine the degree of indistinguishability of single photons and reveal as measured visibilities of $V=0.094(4)$ and $V=0.106(5)$ for excitation pulse separations of 13.1 ns and 5.3 ns, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots grown via molecular beam epitaxy under not experimentally demanding detuned excitation for generating indistinguishable telecom single photons. Further improvements are to be achieved through Purcell enhancement in optical cavities.

AI.tldr: As-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots emitting in the telecom C-band are studied under detuned quasi-resonant excitation, achieving single-photon emission with g^(2)(0)=0.076 and Hong-Ou-Mandel visibilities of ~10% for indistinguishable photons, with potential for cavity-enhanced improvement.
AI.motivation: To investigate as-grown InAsP/InP quantum dots for generating indistinguishable single photons at telecom wavelengths using a simple detuned excitation scheme that suppresses laser scatter while retaining near-resonant advantages.
AI.method: Detuned quasi-resonant excitation (32 meV detuning) was applied to as-grown InAsP/InP QDs grown by MBE. Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT) and Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry were used to measure g^(2)(0) and photon indistinguishability, respectively, at two pulse separations (13.1 ns and 5.3 ns).
AI.result: Raw g^(2)(0)=0.076(6) confirms single-photon emission. HOM visibilities V=0.094(4) for 13.1 ns and V=0.106(5) for 5.3 ns pulse separations, demonstrating partial indistinguishability under detuned excitation.
AI.conclusion: As-grown InAsP/InP QDs under detuned excitation can generate indistinguishable telecom single photons without complex experimental conditions, with further improvements expected via Purcell enhancement in optical cavities.

title: Mean-field Pulse Adaptation for the Circulatization of Interacting Rydberg Atoms
summary: Arrays of circular Rydberg atoms provide a promising platform for quantum simulation and computation; however, their preparation in the presence of interatomic interactions remains a major challenge. While optimal control methods have enabled the design of fast and accurate radio-frequency pulses for the circularization of a single atom and of an atom pair, the extension to more atoms is fundamentally limited by the exponential growth of the Hilbert space, which renders numerical simulations computationally infeasible. Here, we introduce an effective model that treats interactions within a mean-field approximation, thereby enabling the simulation of large atomic systems. Our model further enables the adaptation of pulses optimized for non-interacting atoms to interacting systems, based on the computation of a single time evolution. For two interacting $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ atoms, we demonstrate that the error of our method remains below $1 \, \%$ and that our adapted pulses recover the initial performance of optimal pulses in the regime of weak to moderate interaction strengths.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mean-field effective model to simulate and adapt radio-frequency pulses for circularizing Rydberg atoms in large arrays, overcoming the exponential Hilbert space growth that limits optimal control methods, and demonstrates <1% error for two interacting ⁸⁷Rb atoms with adapted pulses matching optimal performance at weak to moderate interactions.
AI.motivation: Circular Rydberg atom arrays are promising for quantum simulation/computation, but preparing them in the presence of interatomic interactions is a major challenge. Optimal control methods work for single atoms or pairs but are fundamentally limited by exponential Hilbert space growth for larger systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce an effective model that treats interactions within a mean-field approximation, enabling simulation of large atomic systems. They further adapt pulses optimized for non-interacting atoms to interacting systems by computing a single time evolution.
AI.result: For two interacting ⁸⁷Rb atoms, the method achieves <1% error, and the adapted pulses recover the performance of optimal pulses in the weak-to-moderate interaction regime.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field effective model allows scaling to larger atomic arrays while maintaining high fidelity, overcoming the computational infeasibility of direct numerical optimization for many-body systems.

title: Two-state generator extraction: property currents and a two-layer arrow of time in pre- and post-selected quantum dynamics
summary: Conditioning on both past and future assigns intermediate-time properties a causal observer does not; these time-symmetric assignments obey exact symmetry theorems and are measurable from trajectories. We use two-state generator extended dynamic mode decomposition (gEDMD): because weak values obey $dA_w/dt=i\langle[H,A]\rangle_w$ exactly, generator extraction, with an exact-derivative baseline, applies unchanged to them. First, a reflection involution on the pre-/post-selected ensemble splits every window-fitted friction uniquely as $γ_{fwd}=γ_A+γ_S$: $γ_A$, antisymmetric about the midpoint, carries the modes' boundary-condition physics; $γ_S$, symmetric, comes from the differencing scheme; both follow from the same data as $(γ_{fwd}\pmγ_{bwd})/2$. At a fixed inference resolution the arrow of time has two layers: the coherent-mode arrow reverses at the midpoint, the fluctuation-level one does not, $γ_S$ dominating $γ_A$ at every size and class. The difference is one of degree: $γ_S$ is 34 times larger there than at the mode layer, and with the exact derivative both layers reverse: immunity belongs to the inference, not the ensemble. Second, in a lattice interferometer conditioned only at its ports, the quantum Cheshire-cat structure emerges unimposed: particle and polarization obey separate continuity equations, and a local field in the polarization-carrying arm rotates that phase alone, at exactly twice the field strength, entering the generator as a rigid imaginary shift, while the particle's weak density stays invariant to machine precision. We verify the sample-level identity and the two layers from $2^8$ to $2^{20}$ dimensions: $|γ_A|/γ_S=0.09$ to $0.27$ across five classes; self-averaging makes it insensitive to class among those sharing a boundary modulation, removing the $2^{-N/2}$ overlap obstruction for $N$ qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a two-state generator extended dynamic mode decomposition (gEDMD) framework for analyzing time-symmetric quantum dynamics. It shows that pre- and post-selected ensembles yield friction coefficients decomposable into antisymmetric (γ_A) and symmetric (γ_S) components, revealing two layers of the arrow of time: coherent-mode reversal at midpoints while fluctuation-level asymmetry persists. The method also reproduces quantum Cheshire-cat behavior in lattice interferometers without additional assumptions, and demonstrates self-averaging properties across system sizes from 2^8 to 2^20 dimensions.
