AI.motivation: To understand how conditioning on both past and future states assigns different properties to intermediate times compared to causal (past-only) observers, and to develop a framework for extracting time-symmetric dynamics from trajectory data.
AI.method: Two-state generator extended dynamic mode decomposition (gEDMD) applied to weak values, which obey an exact Ehrenfest-like equation dA_w/dt = i⟨[H,A]⟩_w. Friction coefficients are decomposed via a reflection involution on pre-/post-selected ensembles into antisymmetric (γ_A) and symmetric (γ_S) components. The method is tested on lattice interferometers and across system sizes 2^8 to 2^20.
AI.result: The arrow of time has two layers: coherent-mode arrow reverses at the midpoint while fluctuation-level arrow does not; γ_S dominates γ_A by a factor of 34 at the fluctuation layer. Quantum Cheshire-cat structure emerges naturally: particle and polarization obey separate continuity equations, with local field rotating polarization phase at twice the field strength. Across five classes and dimensions 2^8-2^20, |γ_A|/γ_S ranges from 0.09 to 0.27, with self-averaging removing the 2^{-N/2} overlap obstruction.
AI.conclusion: Time-symmetric conditioning reveals a layered arrow of time where immunity to reversal belongs to the inference method rather than the ensemble itself. The gEDMD framework naturally extracts quantum Cheshire-cat behavior and demonstrates self-averaging properties that overcome scalability issues in large qubit systems.

title: Embedded quantum computing for many-body surface reaction
summary: Predictive simulations of catalytic interfaces require correlated electronic-structure treatments that describe localized chemical transformations while retaining the influence of the extended metallic environment. We introduce QC-DFET, a quantum-computing density-functional embedding framework that maps surface-reaction active spaces to compact, environment-aware qubit Hamiltonians. A reaction-consistent active-space protocol preserves orbital continuity along reaction coordinates, while quantum-selected configuration interaction based on measurements from the Zuchongzhi superconducting quantum processor and strongly contracted perturbation theory capture static and dynamic correlation. On Cu(111), QC-DFET treats active spaces up to 28 qubits and is validated through a hierarchy of experimentally constrained surface-chemistry challenges. H2 dissociation/desorption tests balanced bond breaking and recombination barriers, CO adsorption tests site selectivity and metal-adsorbate bonding, and formate hydrogenation tests competing hydrogenation branches with different kinetic and thermodynamic signatures. Across these cases, QC-DFET reproduces bidirectional H2 barriers, recovers the observed top-site preference and adsorption strength of CO, and reconciles the experimentally benchmarked H2COO* reverse barrier with the lower forward barrier to HCOOH*. These results establish embedded quantum computing as a practical route to correlated surface-reaction energetics.

AI.tldr: QC-DFET is a quantum-computing density-functional embedding framework that maps surface-reaction active spaces to compact qubit Hamiltonians, enabling correlated electronic-structure calculations for catalytic interfaces. Validated on Cu(111) across H2 dissociation, CO adsorption, and formate hydrogenation, it reproduces experimental barriers, site preferences, and reaction energetics using up to 28 qubits on the Zuchongzhi superconducting quantum processor.
AI.motivation: Predictive simulations of catalytic interfaces require correlated electronic-structure methods that can describe localized chemical transformations while accounting for the extended metallic environment, which is computationally challenging for conventional approaches.
AI.method: The framework combines density-functional embedding (DFET) with quantum computing: a reaction-consistent active-space protocol preserves orbital continuity along reaction coordinates, and quantum-selected configuration interaction (based on Zuchongzhi quantum processor measurements) plus strongly contracted perturbation theory capture static and dynamic correlation.
AI.result: On Cu(111), QC-DFET treats active spaces up to 28 qubits. It reproduces bidirectional H2 barriers, recovers the observed top-site preference and adsorption strength of CO, and reconciles the experimentally benchmarked H2COO* reverse barrier with the lower forward barrier to HCOOH*.
AI.conclusion: Embedded quantum computing is established as a practical route to correlated surface-reaction energetics, validated through a hierarchy of experimentally constrained surface-chemistry challenges.

title: Finite size scaling of bitstring probability distributions for Rydberg arrays
summary: We calculate the probabilities $p_{\{n\}}$ of the measured bitstrings $\{n\}$ for the vacuum of Rydberg ladders with $N_q$ atoms. As $N_q$ increases, the $p_{\{n\}}$ decrease but become more dense in the low $p$ region raising the possibility that their smallness could be compensated by their large number. The importance of the low probability states can be estimated from the cumulative probability distribution $Σ(p_Λ,N_q)$, which is the probability to observe any state having a probability $p\leq p_Λ$. For not too large values of $p_Λ$, it is possible to approximately collapse the $Σ(p_Λ,N_q)$ for successive $N_q$ into a function resembling the Fermi function when plotted as a function of $-\ln(p_Λ)$. We show that the number of shots necessary to reduce $Σ(p_Λ,N_q)$ to some low enough value grows exponentially with $N_q$. We discuss the implications for calculating observables associated with the vacuum.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the probability distribution of measured bitstrings for the vacuum state of Rydberg ladders, finding that as system size increases, low-probability states become more numerous. The cumulative probability distribution collapses to a Fermi-function-like form, but the number of measurements needed to capture low-probability states grows exponentially with atom number.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the increasing number of low-probability bitstrings (arising from vacuum fluctuations in larger Rydberg systems) can compensate for their individual small probabilities, and to assess the implications for accurately computing observables.
AI.method: Calculates bitstring probabilities $p_{\{n\}}$ for Rydberg ladder vacua with $N_q$ atoms. Analyzes the cumulative probability distribution $\Sigma(p_\Lambda, N_q)$ and demonstrates data collapse onto a Fermi-function-like shape using $-\ln(p_\Lambda)$ scaling. Estimates the required number of experimental shots as a function of $N_q$.
AI.result: The cumulative distribution $\Sigma(p_\Lambda, N_q)$ collapses approximately to a Fermi-function form. However, the number of shots needed to reduce $\Sigma$ to a given low value grows exponentially with the number of atoms $N_q$.
AI.conclusion: The exponential growth in required shots with $N_q$ imposes a fundamental sampling challenge for measuring vacuum observables in larger Rydberg ladders, as the proliferation of low-probability states cannot be efficiently compensated by increased measurements.

title: Reliability Functions of Quantum Soft Covering and Privacy Amplification via a Mixed-Order Rényi Divergence
summary: In this paper, we introduce a novel mixed-order Rényi divergence and investigate its fundamental properties. Using this divergence, we define a family of mixed-order order-two Rényi mutual information and Rényi conditional entropy. We derive exact reliability functions of quantum soft covering and privacy amplification under the sandwiched Rényi divergence with order $α\in[2,\infty)$. The former is jointly characterized by the sandwiched and mixed-order order-two Rényi mutual information quantities, while the latter is characterized by the corresponding conditional entropies. These results provide operational interpretations of the proposed mixed-order Rényi divergence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first exact characterization of the reliability function for quantum soft covering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a mixed-order Rényi divergence, defines related mutual information and conditional entropy, and derives exact reliability functions for quantum soft covering and privacy amplification using sandwiched Rényi divergence with order α∈[2,∞), providing the first exact characterization of the reliability function for quantum soft covering.
AI.motivation: To provide a conceptual framework and exact analytical characterization for fundamental quantum information processing tasks—specifically quantum soft covering and privacy amplification—by introducing a novel mixed-order Rényi divergence that enables precise reliability function derivations.
AI.method: The paper introduces a novel mixed-order Rényi divergence, uses it to define mixed-order order-two Rényi mutual information and conditional entropy, and derives exact reliability functions for quantum soft covering and privacy amplification under the sandwiched Rényi divergence with order α∈[2,∞).
AI.result: The reliability function for quantum soft covering is jointly characterized by the sandwiched and mixed-order order-two Rényi mutual information; the reliability function for privacy amplification is characterized by the corresponding conditional entropies. This is the first exact characterization of the reliability function for quantum soft covering.
AI.conclusion: The mixed-order Rényi divergence gains operational interpretations through its role in exactly characterizing the reliability functions of quantum soft covering and privacy amplification, marking a significant theoretical advancement in quantum information theory.

title: Quantum random-number generator with non-demolition measurements: semi-device-independent implementation
summary: We propose and analyze a novel quantum random-number generator based on a tripartite quantum system in which two subsystems act as detectors. Within a quantum non-demolition measurement scheme, one detector is used to certify the presence of genuine quantum effects in the system's evolution, while the second generates random numbers from a distribution that can be optimized to maximize their entropy. Using one two-level system and two three-level systems, we generate random numbers from a nearly uniform three-outcome distribution, yielding close-to-maximal entropy and therefore near-optimal randomness generation. A key feature of the protocol is that randomness generation and certification occur simultaneously. Moreover, certification does not rely on spacelike separation between detectors, removing a major constraint of device-independent approaches. This property enables practical implementation and facilitates the miniaturization of the device, making the protocol a promising candidate for scalable quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: A novel quantum random-number generator using a tripartite system with two detectors: one certifies genuine quantum effects via QND measurement, the other generates near-uniform random numbers with close-to-maximal entropy. Randomness generation and certification occur simultaneously without requiring spacelike separation, enabling practical miniaturization.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum random-number generator that overcomes the major practical constraint of device-independent approaches (spacelike separation between detectors) while still providing certification of genuine quantum randomness, enabling scalable and miniaturized implementations.
AI.method: A tripartite quantum system (one two-level system + two three-level systems) within a quantum non-demolition measurement scheme. One detector certifies genuine quantum effects, while the second generates random numbers from an optimized distribution. The protocol uses QND measurements to enable simultaneous certification and generation without spacelike separation.
AI.result: Generation of random numbers from a nearly uniform three-outcome distribution, yielding close-to-maximal entropy and near-optimal randomness generation. Certification and randomness generation occur simultaneously without requiring spacelike separation between detectors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol removes a major constraint of device-independent approaches (spacelike separation), enabling practical implementation and device miniaturization, making it a promising candidate for scalable quantum technologies.

title: Unconventional Thermalization of a Three-Wave-Mixing Model
summary: Understanding the boundaries between quantum thermalization and localization in many-body systems remains a central frontier of condensed matter and quantum information science. In this work, we investigate the dynamics and spectral properties of a generic model with long-range three-body-interaction, namely, a system with non-local three-wave-mixing. This model has been realized recently with a microwave Fabry-Perot cavity terminated on one end by a superconducting qubit mirror. Utilizing exact diagonalization techniques, we uncover a striking paradox: the global energy level spacing statistics show integrability, even though all dynamic observables and inverse participation ratios of the eigenstates indicate ergodicity and delocalization. We show that this behavior is a hallmark of strong Hilbert space fragmentation driven by kinematic constraints rather than an explicit global symmetry. Inside these sectors, dynamics scramble rapidly, as evidenced by the out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC), while global transport is heavily bottlenecked, resulting in a logarithmic relaxation to equilibrium. This picture is further confirmed by fluctuations in eigenstate entanglement entropy at the same energy. Finally, we demonstrate that the late time OTOC average scales with system size, providing a distinct experimentally accessible signature of the underlying three-body kinetic bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a model with long-range three-body interactions, revealing that despite global level statistics suggesting integrability, dynamic observables indicate ergodicity and delocalization due to strong Hilbert space fragmentation from kinematic constraints. This leads to rapid scrambling within sectors but slow global transport with logarithmic relaxation.
AI.motivation: To understand the boundaries between quantum thermalization and localization in many-body systems, particularly the role of long-range three-body interactions and emerging phenomena like Hilbert space fragmentation without explicit symmetries.
AI.method: Exact diagonalization of a generic model with long-range three-body-wave-mixing, realized in a microwave Fabry-Perot cavity terminated by a superconducting qubit mirror. Analysis includes level spacing statistics, inverse participation ratios (IPRs), out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOC), and eigenstate entanglement entropy.
AI.result: Global level spacing statistics indicate integrability, while IPRs and dynamic observables show ergodicity/delocalization. Hilbert space fragmentation due to kinematic constraints causes rapid scrambling within sectors but bottlenecked global transport with logarithmic relaxation. Late-time OTOC scales with system size.
AI.conclusion: The observed behavior is a hallmark of strong Hilbert space fragmentation driven by kinematic constraints, not global symmetry. Late-time OTOC scaling provides an experimentally accessible signature of three-body kinetic bottlenecks.

title: Quasi-polar Decomposition of Quantum Neural Networks via Adaptive Non-local Observables
summary:
We use Diagonal Adaptive Non-local Observables (DANO) as a canonical decomposition for studying Variational Quantum Circuit model evolution. Separating each learned observable into a diagonal spectrum and a unitary basis gives a quasi-polar description: the spectral weights are viewed as radial coordinates, while the unitary circuit serves as angular coordinates through Lie group identifications. This turns the training process into a trajectory in spectral and Lie-algebra space.
  Experiments on two classification tasks show that DANO radial spectral expansion correlates with accuracy. DANO angle coordinates reveal a dominant accuracy-correlated component. The framework provides a different perspective to characterize quantum model behavior.

AI.tldr: DANO decomposes quantum observables into diagonal spectra (radial) and unitary circuits (angular), showing spectral expansion correlates with accuracy in classification tasks.
AI.motivation: To provide a canonical decomposition framework for studying variational quantum circuit model evolution, offering a geometric perspective on training dynamics.
AI.method: Uses Diagonal Adaptive Non-local Observables (DANO) to separate each learned observable into a diagonal spectrum (radial coordinates) and a unitary basis (angular coordinates via Lie group), transforming training into a trajectory in spectral and Lie-algebra space.
AI.result: DANO radial spectral expansion correlates with accuracy, and angle coordinates reveal a dominant accuracy-correlated component on two classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: The DANO framework provides a new perspective for characterizing quantum model behavior through spectral and angular coordinates.

title: Optimising Trotter-Suzuki Simulations of Markovian Open Quantum Systems via Classical Search
summary: Simulating an open quantum system on a digital quantum computer often involves the use of Trotter-Suzuki (TS) Product Formulas (PF) to approximate the system's time evolution. Precise estimates for the required number of Trotter steps (and hence the overall gate count) can be crucial for minimising the computational cost of these methods. Building on established theoretical guarantees, we derive analytic bounds for the First- and Second-Order Deterministic and Randomised TS-PF, directly relating the number of Trotter steps to the model parameters, evolution time and precision. These bounds enable concrete resource estimation for each method. We then present a computationally efficient classical algorithm that uses diamond norm estimates of individual Liouvillian terms and a binary search to significantly reduce the Trotter steps required for a target precision. Our numerical results on two prototypical models - an XX-Spin Chain with boundary driving and local dephasing, and a Transverse-Field Ising Model - show that the theoretical (analytic) bounds are often overly conservative, whereas the empirical (optimised) bounds yield a significantly smaller number of Trotter steps for the same precision. Among the methods investigated, the Second-Order Randomised TS-PF typically achieves the lowest resource demands, especially for larger systems. These findings emphasise the significance of empirical bounding strategies in achieving more resource-efficient simulations of Markovian open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper derives analytic Trotter-step bounds for First- and Second-Order Deterministic and Randomised Trotter-Suzuki Product Formulas for open quantum systems, and proposes a classical algorithm using diamond-norm estimates and binary search to compute tighter empirical bounds. Numerical tests on two models show analytic bounds are overly conservative, while empirical bounds significantly reduce required Trotter steps, with Second-Order Randomised TS-PF being the most resource-efficient.
AI.motivation: Minimising the computational cost (gate count) of simulating open quantum systems on digital quantum computers by deriving precise estimates for the number of Trotter steps required.
AI.method: Derived analytic bounds for First- and Second-Order Deterministic and Randomised TS-PF linking Trotter steps to model parameters, time, and precision. Developed a classical algorithm using diamond-norm estimates of individual Liouvillian terms combined with binary search to compute tighter empirical bounds.
AI.result: Analytic bounds are overly conservative; empirical bounds yield significantly fewer Trotter steps. Second-Order Randomised TS-PF achieves the lowest resource demands, especially for larger systems.
AI.conclusion: Empirical bounding strategies are crucial for resource-efficient simulations of Markovian open quantum systems, with Second-Order Randomised TS-PF being the most efficient.

title: Adaptive Multi-Backend Simulation of Near-Clifford Quantum Circuits via Spatial Stabilizer-Frame Partitioning
summary:
We present an exact amplitude simulator for Clifford+T quantum circuits that combines a Feynman path sum across a balanced qubit bipartition with stabilizer-frame simulation on each half. The construction extends prior stabilizer-based Schrödinger-Feynman methods in three directions: recursive multilevel bipartition into a binary tree, automatic fallback to dense state-vector simulation when a leaf's stabilizer frame would exceed its memory ceiling, and a cost-model-driven partition selector that replaces the standard cut-count minimization heuristic.
  We show cut-count minimization is an unreliable proxy in practice: a globally cleaner partition can reduce cross-cut count yet increase wall-clock time, because it imbalances T-gate density across halves and inflates per-half stabilizer-frame size. Our cost model substitutes the stabilizer-frame bound 2w for the dense 2n ceiling per side and explicitly models per-amplitude readout cost; isolating that term uncovered a quadratic-asymptotic inefficiency in the leaf simulator's end-of-path amplitude extraction, fixed by replacing it with an existing O(F * s * n) single-amplitude inner product.
  On a structured hierarchical n=16 benchmark the recursive simulator beats monolithic stabilizer-frame simulation by 92x to 17,645x, wins by 79x per path against a dense half-state-vector baseline under an identical cut, and beats a production state-vector simulator end to end by up to 47.9x (median ~5x). On adversarial random Clifford+T circuits the dense state vector wins past a crossover near n/2 cross-cut gates -- the regime the cost model identifies. The dominant cost, the cross-cut Feynman sum, is embarrassingly parallel with constant inter-worker communication, unlike recent matrix-product-state stabilizer-tensor methods whose inner contraction loop is sequential.

AI.tldr: A recursive stabilizer-frame simulator for Clifford+T circuits that combines Feynman path summation across a qubit bipartition with stabilizer simulation on each half, featuring a cost-model-driven partition selector (replacing cut-count minimization), automatic fallback to dense simulation, and a fix for quadratic-asymptotic inefficiency in leaf amplitude extraction. Achieves up to 17,645x speedup over monolithic stabilizer-frame simulation on hierarchical benchmarks and up to 47.9x over production state-vector simulators.
AI.motivation: Existing stabilizer-based Schrödinger-Feynman methods lack multilevel recursion, adaptive fallback to dense simulation, and reliable partition heuristics. Cut-count minimization is shown to be an unreliable proxy for actual runtime, motivating a cost-model-driven selector that accounts for T-gate density imbalance and stabilizer-frame size.
AI.method: Combines Feynman path sum across a balanced qubit bipartition with stabilizer-frame simulation on each half. Extends prior work with: (1) recursive multilevel bipartition into a binary tree, (2) automatic fallback to dense state-vector simulation when leaf stabilizer frame exceeds memory, (3) cost-model-driven partition selector replacing cut-count minimization. The cost model substitutes stabilizer-frame bound 2^w for dense 2^n ceiling and models per-amplitude readout cost, revealing and fixing a quadratic-asymptotic inefficiency replaced by O(F·s·n) single-amplitude inner product.
AI.result: On hierarchical n=16 benchmark: 92x–17,645x speedup vs monolithic stabilizer-frame simulation, 79x per-path improvement vs dense half-state-vector baseline, up to 47.9x (median ~5x) vs production state-vector simulator. On random Clifford+T circuits, dense state vector wins past crossover near n/2 cross-cut gates. The cross-cut Feynman sum is embarrassingly parallel with constant inter-worker communication.
AI.conclusion: The recursive stabilizer-frame simulator with cost-model-driven partitioning significantly outperforms prior methods on structured benchmarks, though dense simulation remains competitive for random circuits above a crossover point. The dominant cost is embarrassingly parallel, offering strong scalability advantages over sequential matrix-product-state stabilizer-tensor methods.

title: Native CCZ Gate with Fluxonium Qubits and a Microwave-Driven Coupler
summary: Native multi-qubit gates could reduce the overhead associated with decompositions into single- and two-qubit operations, but whether they can simultaneously provide high fidelity, simple control and robustness against parasitic interactions in scalable architectures remains unclear. Here we experimentally realize a 65-ns native controlled-controlled-phase operation, locally equivalent to the Toffoli gate, with a fidelity of 99.39(5)% in a three-qubit processor unit based on fluxonium qubits coupled via a microwave-driven transmon coupler. The implemented operation would require CZ fidelities of approximately 99.94% if realized through a conventional decomposition. The gate is implemented with a single control pulse, that relies on a simple calibration procedure yielding coherence-limited performance. This processor unit naturally extends to scalable two-dimensional layouts with low parasitic interactions. Altogether, these results establish native multi-qubit gates as a viable hardware-efficient primitive for scalable superconducting quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates a 65-ns native Toffoli (controlled-controlled-phase) gate in a fluxonium-based three-qubit processor with 99.39% fidelity, using a single control pulse via a microwave-driven transmon coupler, showing that native multi-qubit gates can be hardware-efficient and scalable.
AI.motivation: To determine whether native multi-qubit gates can simultaneously achieve high fidelity, simple control, and robustness against parasitic interactions in scalable superconducting architectures, addressing the question of whether they can reduce decomposition overhead compared to conventional single- and two-qubit gate decompositions.
AI.method: The gate is implemented using three fluxonium qubits coupled via a microwave-driven transmon coupler, with a single control pulse and a simple calibration procedure. The native controlled-controlled-phase gate (equivalent to Toffoli) operates in 65 ns and is benchmarked via fidelity measurements.
AI.result: The native Toffoli gate achieves a fidelity of 99.39(5)%, which would require CZ fidelities of approximately 99.94% if realized through conventional decomposition. The design naturally extends to scalable 2D layouts with low parasitic interactions.
AI.conclusion: Native multi-qubit gates are a viable, hardware-efficient primitive for scalable superconducting quantum processors, offering coherence-limited performance with simple calibration and reduced overhead.

title: Effective Hamiltonians for Predictive Quantum Control
summary: High-fidelity quantum control relies on accurate models of driven dynamics. We examine this re- quirement for single-qubit gates in superconducting transmons by comparing control pulses derived from the standard Duffing approximation and from a Hamiltonian constructed by diagonalizing the transmon eigenbasis. Using the same correction-pulse construction for both models, we show that correction fields derived from the Duffing approximation can substantially reduce the gate error pre- dicted by that model while remaining less effective when combined with an independently calibrated baseline pulse in the diagonalized-transmon model. In the fast-gate regime, such transferred correc- tions can even fail to improve over the uncorrected diagonalized-transmon baseline. We show that small model-dependent differences in both the energy spectrum and the representation of the drive operator can compound during driven evolution, resulting in different predicted error generators and correction pulses. A mismatch in the accumulated AC Stark phase provides one illustrative di- agnostic of this dynamical model dependence. We further demonstrate that the model Hamiltonian informs the choice of control framework: Omitting relevant leakage pathways or higher-order error channels can lead to an overly restricted correction strategy. Including these channels motivates an extended correction framework that improves the gate performance using the same physical control resources.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the standard Duffing approximation for transmon qubits produces different predicted dynamics and optimal correction pulses compared to a more accurate diagonalized-transmon model. Small differences in energy spectra and drive operators compound during evolution, leading to model-dependent gate errors. The authors demonstrate that correction pulses derived from the Duffing model transfer poorly to the more accurate model, especially in the fast-gate regime, and that omitting relevant leakage or higher-order error channels restricts correction effectiveness.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity quantum control requires accurate models of driven dynamics. The authors want to examine how well the standard Duffing approximation captures the true dynamics of superconducting transmon qubits, and whether control pulses derived from this approximation remain effective when applied to a more accurate Hamiltonian model.
AI.method: The authors compare control pulses derived from two models: (1) the standard Duffing approximation, and (2) a Hamiltonian constructed by diagonalizing the transmon eigenbasis. They use the same correction-pulse construction for both models and test transferability of corrections. They analyze differences in energy spectra, drive operator representation, error generators, and AC Stark phase accumulation. They also examine how model choice informs control framework design regarding leakage and higher-order error channels.
AI.result: Correction fields from the Duffing approximation reduce gate error in that model but are less effective in the diagonalized-transmon model. In the fast-gate regime, transferred corrections can fail to improve over the uncorrected baseline. Small model-dependent differences in energy spectrum and drive operator representation compound during driven evolution, producing different predicted error generators. A mismatch in accumulated AC Stark phase serves as a diagnostic of this model dependence. Including relevant leakage pathways and higher-order error channels motivates an extended correction framework that improves performance with the same physical resources.
AI.conclusion: Accurate modeling of driven transmon dynamics matters for high-fidelity control; the Duffing approximation has systematic limitations that affect correction-pulse design. Model Hamiltonian choice informs the control framework — omitting relevant error channels restricts correction strategies. An extended framework accounting for leakage and higher-order errors yields better gate performance without additional physical resources.

title: Ky Fan majorization for binary tensor products
summary: We provide a short proof of a Ky Fan-type majorization relation for the singular values of a sum of binary tensor products of matrices. This generalizes Alhejji's result (arXiv:2410.18254) from two summands to arbitrary sums and from positive matrices to arbitrary matrices. As an application, we show a majorization relation between the singular values of a completely positive map and those of its Kraus operators.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a short proof of a Ky Fan-type majorization relation for singular values of sums of binary tensor products of matrices, generalizing a previous result from two summands to arbitrary sums and from positive to arbitrary matrices. It also shows a majorization relation between singular values of completely positive maps and their Kraus operators.
AI.motivation: To generalize Alhejji's result (arXiv:2410.18254) on Ky Fan-type majorization from two summands to arbitrary sums and from positive matrices to arbitrary matrices.
AI.method: A short proof of a Ky Fan-type majorization relation for the singular values of a sum of binary tensor products of matrices.
AI.result: Generalization of Alhejji's result to arbitrary sums and arbitrary matrices, and a majorization relation between singular values of completely positive maps and their Kraus operators.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a broader applicability of Ky Fan-type majorization relations in matrix analysis and quantum information theory.

title: The Keyl-Werner algorithm is not optimal for spectrum estimation
summary:
We give an algorithm which, given $n = O(d^2 \cdot (\log\log(d)/\log(d))^2)$ copies of $ρ$, estimates the eigenvalues of $ρ$ to constant error in total variation distance. Thus, we can learn the eigenvalues of a quantum state with fewer copies than the $Θ(d^2)$ needed to run full state tomography. This is the first improvement to spectrum estimation over the influential Keyl-Werner algorithm, which uses $n = Θ(d^2)$ copies, thereby resolving a question raised by Keyl and Werner in 2001 and refuting a 2016 conjecture of Wright.
  Our main technical tool is a new tomography guarantee, where the error of tomography in a particular direction $|w\rangle$ scales with $\langle w | ρ|w\rangle$ for all directions simultaneously. From this stronger "relative-error" bound, we recover better algorithms for principal component analysis in Bures distance and tomography in $χ^2$-divergence as corollaries.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an algorithm that estimates the eigenvalues of a quantum state using only n = O(d² · (log log d / log d)²) copies, improving over the Θ(d²) needed for full state tomography and the Keyl-Werner algorithm, resolving a 2001 open question and refuting a 2016 conjecture. The key technique is a relative-error tomography bound, yielding corollaries for PCA in Bures distance and tomography in χ²-divergence.
AI.motivation: To determine whether eigenvalue estimation of a quantum state requires asymptotically fewer copies than full state tomography (Θ(d²)), resolving a question posed by Keyl and Werner in 2001 and refuting a 2016 conjecture by Wright.
AI.method: The main technical tool is a new tomography guarantee that provides a relative-error bound: the error in estimating ρ along any direction |w⟩ scales with ⟨w|ρ|w⟩ simultaneously for all directions, rather than a uniform absolute error bound.
AI.result: The algorithm uses n = O(d² · (log log d / log d)²) copies to estimate eigenvalues to constant total variation error, which is asymptotically fewer than the Θ(d²) copies required by the Keyl-Werner algorithm and full state tomography.
AI.conclusion: Spectrum estimation can be performed with strictly fewer copies than full state tomography, resolving the long-standing open question, and the relative-error tomography technique yields improved algorithms for PCA in Bures distance and tomography in χ²-divergence.

title: Hardware-efficient erasure-error detection with an integer fluxonium
summary: Erasure-error detection can improve the efficiency of quantum error correction by revealing the times and locations of their error events. In this work, we demonstrate erasure conversions and mid-circuit erasure detections in a single integer fluxonium, in which the states $\mathrm{|g\rangle, |f\rangle}$ encode the logical states and $\mathrm{|e\rangle}$ encodes the erasure state. The integer fluxonium suppresses direct $|\mathrm{f} \rangle \rightarrow |\mathrm{g} \rangle$ transitions and allows the dominant $|\mathrm{f} \rangle \rightarrow |\mathrm{e}\rangle$ transitions to be converted into detectable erasures. Furthermore, we identified a design space that nullifies the resonant-frequency shift between the two logical states, enabling ancilla-free mid-circuit erasure checks using the same resonator employed for final readout. By discarding the detected erasure events, we achieved an 8.4-fold increase in the $|\mathrm{f}\rangle$ state lifetime, a 1.38-fold increase in the Hahn-echo time, and a reduction of single-qubit gate error from 0.061(2)% to 0.030(5)%. Our results establish integer fluxonium as a hardware-efficient platform for erasure-error detection and conversion, while identifying the improvements required to realize an effective erasure qubit with high erasure bias.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates erasure-error detection and conversion in a single integer fluxonium qubit, where states |g⟩ and |f⟩ encode logical information and |e⟩ serves as the erasure state. By detecting and discarding erasure events, the authors achieved significant improvements in qubit lifetime (8.4x), coherence time (1.38x), and gate fidelity (error reduced from 0.061% to 0.030%).
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency of quantum error correction by implementing erasure-error detection, which reveals the times and locations of error events, in a hardware-efficient platform.
AI.method: The authors use an integer fluxonium qubit with three states: |g⟩ and |f⟩ as logical states, and |e⟩ as the erasure state. They suppress direct |f⟩→|g⟩ transitions and convert dominant |f⟩→|e⟩ transitions into detectable erasures. They also designed a bias scheme that nullifies the resonant-frequency shift between logical states, enabling ancilla-free mid-circuit erasure checks using the same readout resonator.
AI.result: 8.4-fold increase in |f⟩ state lifetime, 1.38-fold increase in Hahn-echo time, and reduction of single-qubit gate error from 0.061(2)% to 0.030(5)% by discarding detected erasure events.
AI.conclusion: Integer fluxonium is established as a hardware-efficient platform for erasure-error detection and conversion, with identified improvements needed for realizing an effective erasure qubit with high erasure bias.

title: Parity-Based Time-Bin Encoding Enabling SWAP Between Polarization and Time-Bin Qubits
summary: Multi-degree-of-freedom photonic quantum processing requires routing between degree-of-freedom (DOF) qubit encodings on a single photon. A SWAP between polarization and time-bin qubits is Multi-degree-of-freedom photonic quantum processing requires routing between degree-of-freedom (DOF) qubit encodings on a single photon. A SWAP between polarization and time-bin qubits is an advantageous primitive for such architectures, however conventional early/late time-bin encoding does not support bidirectional logical time-bin flips from late to early which limits the ability to implement certain quantum operations. We introduce a parity-based time-bin encoding in which logical $\vert 0 \rangle_T$ and $\vert 1 \rangle_T$ correspond to even and odd multiples of a spacing $Δt$, so that a physical delay of $Δt$ implements $\vert 0 \rangle_T \leftrightarrow \vert 1 \rangle_T$. This encoding is the enabling ingredient that makes a polarization-controlled delay line implement $\mathrm{CNOT}_{P \rightarrow T}$ and aligns naturally with periodic refractive index modulation for $\mathrm{CNOT}_{T \rightarrow P}$. Composing three such CNOT operations sequentially results in a deterministic SWAP between polarization and time-bin degrees of freedom. We analyze field-based modulation polarization-rotation error probability and timing-resolution constraints set by both EOM drive electronics and photon detection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a parity-based time-bin encoding that enables a deterministic SWAP operation between polarization and time-bin qubits, overcoming limitations of conventional early/late encoding by using even/odd multiples of a spacing Δt, and analyzes error probabilities and timing constraints.
AI.motivation: Multi-DOF photonic quantum processing requires routing between different DOF qubit encodings on a single photon. A SWAP between polarization and time-bin qubits is a useful primitive, but conventional early/late time-bin encoding cannot support bidirectional logical time-bin flips (late to early), limiting certain quantum operations.
AI.method: Proposes a parity-based time-bin encoding where logical |0⟩_T and |1⟩_T correspond to even and odd multiples of spacing Δt, enabling physical delay Δt to implement |0⟩_T ↔ |1⟩_T. This encoding makes a polarization-controlled delay line implement CNOT_{P→T} and aligns with periodic refractive index modulation for CNOT_{T→P}. Three sequential CNOT operations yield a deterministic SWAP.
AI.result: The parity-based encoding enables both CNOT_{P→T} and CNOT_{T→P} operations, and their sequential composition achieves a deterministic polarization-time-bin SWAP. Field-based modulation polarization-rotation error probability and timing-resolution constraints from EOM drive electronics and photon detection are analyzed.
AI.conclusion: The parity-based time-bin encoding overcomes the limitations of conventional encoding for implementing SWAP between polarization and time-bin DOFs, providing a viable primitive for multi-DOF photonic quantum processing.

title: Improved Methods for Determining Quantum Error Correcting Code Performance and Fault Tolerance
summary: One of the central challenges in quantum error correction is determining the performance of a code in the low-error regimes needed to implement utility-scale computations. While performance at these error rates is not amenable to direct Monte Carlo simulation, it can be extrapolated from simulations at higher logical error rates, assuming the logical error rate scales predictably with increasing distance or decreasing physical error rate. However, the expected scaling depends sensitively on the minimum weight of uncorrectable error patterns. In many cases, the minimum weight is unknown since it depends not only on the theoretical code distance, but also on details of the implementation. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods, as adapted to quantum error correction by Bravyi and Vargo, provide a way to estimate logical failure rates in these low-error regimes via simulation. While offering significant gains over Monte Carlo, the described Metropolis algorithm makes small changes to the current logical failure patterns which results in slow convergence. In this paper, we argue that typical failure patterns include a large number of easily correctable errors that coexist alongside a malignant core. This observation motivates two new approaches to better evaluate code performance. First, we describe a pruning algorithm designed to obviate these correctable errors and focus on the problematic low-weight core. Second, we develop a novel family of Metropolis-Hastings algorithms, referred to as subregion MCMC. This technique is parameterized by the fraction of the error pattern that is resampled at each step, effectively interpolating between Monte Carlo and single step MCMC. We show that a judicious choice of this parameter results in far faster convergence than prior work.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes two new MCMC-based methods (pruning algorithm and subregion MCMC) to more efficiently estimate logical error rates in quantum error correction, addressing the slow convergence of prior Metropolis-based approaches by recognizing that typical failure patterns contain many easily correctable errors alongside a malignant core.
AI.motivation: Determining code performance in low-error regimes needed for utility-scale quantum computation is challenging because direct Monte Carlo simulation is intractable, and existing MCMC methods suffer from slow convergence due to small incremental changes to error patterns.
AI.method: (1) A pruning algorithm that removes easily correctable errors to focus on the low-weight malignant core; (2) A subregion MCMC family parameterized by the fraction of the error pattern resampled at each step, interpolating between Monte Carlo and single-step MCMC.
AI.result: Judicious choice of the subregion MCMC parameter results in far faster convergence than prior work.
AI.conclusion: The proposed techniques significantly improve the efficiency of logical failure rate estimation for quantum error correcting codes at low error rates, enabling better performance assessment for utility-scale quantum computation.

title: Training Quantum Dragons
summary: The Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) is the standard formalism for nano-scale electron transport. By recasting the NEGF scattering problem as a linear system of equations whose solution encodes the transmission and reflection amplitudes, we present the first quantum computerized implementation of NEGF. We apply both the Harrow--Hassidim--Lloyd and Variational Quantum Linear Solver algorithms to compute the transmission coefficient $T(E)$ of quantum dragon nanodevices within the single-band tight-binding model. Quantum dragon devices exhibit perfect transmission across the full conducting band regardless of internal disorder. The problem maps onto compact circuits of 3 and 4 total physical qubits for the 2-site and 6-site dragon devices, respectively. A similarity transformation block-diagonalizes the NEGF linear system reducing the Pauli decomposition of the block-encoded matrix. We demonstrate the feasibility of quantum computation by performing ideal and noise-aware simulations and computations on physical IBM quantum processor.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first quantum computer implementation of Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism for nano-scale electron transport, using HHL and VQLS algorithms to compute transmission coefficients of quantum dragon nanodevices on IBM quantum processors with up to 4 qubits.
AI.motivation: To enable quantum computation of NEGF scattering problems by recasting them as linear systems of equations, potentially offering speedups over classical approaches for simulating nano-scale electron transport.
AI.method: Recast NEGF scattering as a linear system; apply HHL and VQLS algorithms; use quantum dragon devices (2-site and 6-site) within single-band tight-binding model; implement similarity transformation for block-diagonalization to reduce Pauli decomposition; perform ideal, noise-aware simulations and runs on physical IBM quantum processor.
AI.result: Demonstrated feasibility of quantum computation of NEGF transmission coefficients on 3-4 physical qubit circuits for quantum dragon devices, with both ideal/noise-aware simulations and physical IBM processor runs.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computation of NEGF is feasible on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware for small systems, with the block-diagonalization technique reducing circuit complexity.

title: OQRAM: Oblivious Quantum Random Access Memory for Securing Delegated Quantum Queries
summary: Quantum query is a basic subroutine in many quantum algorithms, and Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) provides a natural way to realize such coherent query access. In delegated settings, however, a standard QRAM query interface can expose sensitive information to the server. This paper introduces oblivious QRAM, a cryptographic abstraction for privacy-preserving delegated coherent query access. The protocol consists of an offline refresh phase and an online protected query phase. The database is stored in an encrypted and shuffled layout, and each query is protected by coherent address masking using either a quantum-secure pseudorandom permutation (qPRP) based method or a quantum one-time pad (qOTP) based method. In the adopted client model, the online protection adds only modest quantum overhead beyond the query register, avoiding the exponential quantum resources that would otherwise be required by an equivalent local QRAM construction. The qPRP-based variant also supports multi-query use by distributing database refresh across multiple queries to reduce classical communication. To address malicious servers, decoy checks are further incorporated to strengthen privacy protection and enable probabilistic tampering detection. Compared with fully blind quantum computing, this framework provides a lighter abstraction tailored to private delegated QRAM access, significantly reducing quantum resource requirements on both the client and server sides and achieving an exponential reduction in quantum communication.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces oblivious QRAM, a cryptographic framework for privacy-preserving delegated quantum query access that uses encrypted/shuffled database layouts and coherent address masking (via qPRP or qOTP), achieving modest quantum overhead for clients and exponential reduction in quantum communication compared to fully blind quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Standard QRAM query interfaces in delegated settings can expose sensitive information to the server. The paper aims to provide a privacy-preserving abstraction for delegated coherent quantum queries without requiring exponential quantum resources.
AI.method: The protocol consists of an offline refresh phase and an online protected query phase. The database is stored in an encrypted and shuffled layout. Address queries are protected via coherent address masking using either a quantum-secure pseudorandom permutation (qPRP) or quantum one-time pad (qOTP). Decoy checks are incorporated for malicious server resilience.
AI.result: Online protection adds only modest quantum overhead beyond the query register, avoiding exponential quantum resources. The qPRP variant supports multi-query use with distributed refresh to reduce classical communication. The framework achieves exponential reduction in quantum communication compared to fully blind quantum computing.
AI.conclusion: Oblivious QRAM provides a lighter, more efficient abstraction for private delegated QRAM access, significantly reducing quantum resource requirements on both client and server sides while enabling probabilistic tampering detection against malicious servers.

title: Classical and Quantum MacWilliams Transforms as Spin Kinematics
summary: Spin is the hidden engine behind the zoo of MacWilliams transforms in weight enumerator theories - not only for qubits and qudits, but even for classical codes. From nothing more than a split into trivial and nontrivial errors, we kinematically derive the MacWilliams transform as a Wigner-$D$ rotation between two canonical bases. Within each classical and quantum theory, changing the length $n$ leaves the rotation untouched: the same element simply reappears at spin $n/2$. And at fixed $n$, changing the rotation axis simply moves between the various classical and quantum theories.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that MacWilliams transforms in weight enumerator theories arise from a spin-based kinematic framework, where the transform is a Wigner-D rotation between canonical bases. Changing code length n corresponds to changing spin (n/2), while changing the rotation axis transitions between classical and quantum theories.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified kinematic foundation for MacWilliams transforms across classical and quantum error-correcting codes, revealing the underlying spin structure.
AI.method: Derives the MacWilliams transform as a Wigner-D rotation from a split into trivial and nontrivial errors, showing the transform is independent of code length n and depends only on the rotation axis.
AI.result: The MacWilliams transform is a Wigner-D rotation at spin n/2 that remains unchanged when varying length n, and varies between classical/quantum theories when the rotation axis changes.
AI.conclusion: Spin provides a unified kinematic explanation for MacWilliams transforms across all weight enumerator theories, with length and theory type corresponding to spin magnitude and rotation axis respectively.

title: Reconfigurable Optical Platform for One-way Quantum Communication Complexity
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables; includes Supplementary Material
summary: Demonstrating a practical quantum advantage remains a central goal in quantum information science. While quantum computational supremacy is still technologically demanding, communication complexity offers a promising route to showcase quantum advantage with current photonic platforms. Here we introduce a reconfigurable optical platform for one-way quantum communication complexity based on multimode fibers and wavefront shaping. We experimentally validate it by implementing a genuine one-way quantum communication complexity problem for which an exponential quantum--classical communication separation is known. Complementary numerical simulations show that the same reconfigurable decoding architecture can support more general one-way communication tasks with comparable performance, while also offering a route to higher-dimensional implementations without increasing hardware complexity. Together, these results establish multimode-fiber wavefront shaping as a versatile hardware platform for one-way quantum communication complexity and provide a concrete roadmap toward more demanding protocols, where stronger quantum--classical separations could enable practical demonstrations of quantum advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a reconfigurable optical platform using multimode fibers and wavefront shaping for one-way quantum communication complexity, experimentally demonstrating an exponential quantum-classical communication separation, with numerical simulations showing scalability to higher-dimensional tasks.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate practical quantum advantage in communication complexity using current photonic technology, as quantum computational supremacy remains technologically demanding.
AI.method: A reconfigurable optical platform based on multimode fibers and wavefront shaping for one-way quantum communication complexity protocols.
AI.result: Experimental validation of an exponential quantum-classical communication separation; numerical simulations confirm scalability to more general one-way communication tasks and higher-dimensional implementations without increasing hardware complexity.
AI.conclusion: Multimode-fiber wavefront shaping is a versatile hardware platform for one-way quantum communication complexity, offering a concrete roadmap toward stronger quantum-classical separations and practical quantum advantage demonstrations.

title: Robust quantum state certification and uncertainty principles for total influence
summary:
We show that nonadaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements suffice to test whether an unknown $n$-qubit state $ρ$ is $\varepsilon$-close to or $O(\varepsilon)$-far from an ideal target state $|ψ\rangle$, for all but a $2^{-Ω(n)}$ fraction of target states. The test uses $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/δ))$ copies of $ρ$ to achieve confidence $1-δ$, which is information-theoretically optimal even among protocols with arbitrary joint measurements.
  The main technical innovation is an uncertainty principle for weighted generalizations of the total influence of Boolean functions. As a simple example, the unweighted variant states that $\mathbf{Inf}[f]+\mathbf{Inf}[\widehat{f}] = Ω(n)$, which is a natural hypercube analogue of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (here $\widehat{\,\cdot\,}$ denotes the $2^{-n/2}$-normalized Fourier transform). The weighted case generalizes $\mathbf{Inf}[\,\cdot\,]$ and $\mathbf{Inf}[\,\widehat{\,\cdot\,}\,]$ to Dirichlet energies associated with Glauber dynamics for certain dual measures on the cube.

AI.tldr: Nonadaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements can test whether an unknown n-qubit state is close to or far from an ideal target state, using an information-theoretically optimal number of copies, for all but an exponentially small fraction of target states. The key innovation is an uncertainty principle for weighted generalizations of Boolean function influence.
AI.motivation: To develop an efficient, information-theoretically optimal protocol for testing quantum states using only simple single-qubit Pauli measurements, applicable to almost all target states.
AI.method: The paper introduces an uncertainty principle for weighted generalizations of the total influence of Boolean functions. The unweighted variant states that Inf[f] + Inf[f̂] = Ω(n) (a hypercube analogue of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle). The weighted case generalizes influence to Dirichlet energies associated with Glauber dynamics for dual measures on the hypercube.
AI.result: Nonadaptive single-qubit Pauli measurements suffice to distinguish whether ρ is ε-close to or O(ε)-far from |ψ⟩ for all but a 2^{-Ω(n)} fraction of target states. The test uses O(ε^{-2} log(1/δ)) copies, which is information-theoretically optimal even among protocols with arbitrary joint measurements.
AI.conclusion: Simple, nonadaptive Pauli measurements achieve optimal sample complexity for quantum state testing for almost all target states, enabled by a new Fourier-analytic uncertainty principle.

title: Sharp Bounds on Ground State Energy of the SYK Model
summary:
We study the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) Hamiltonian $H_{\operatorname{SYK}}$ on $n$ Majorana modes with $k$-body interactions, and prove that $\mathbb{E}\|H_{\operatorname{SYK}}\|_{\operatorname{op}} = (1 - o(1))\cdot\sqrt{2n}/k$ for super-constant $k\leq o(\sqrt{n})$, where the expectation is over the disorder variables in the Hamiltonian. This confirms the predictions due to Garcia-Garcia, Jia and Verbaarschot'18 and answers a question posed in Feng, Tian and Wei'19. Our results extend to the sparse SYK Hamiltonian. As a corollary, we obtain that the dissipative quantum algorithm of Basso, Chen and Dalzell'24 provably computes the ground state energy of the SYK Hamiltonian up to an $O(1)$-multiplicative factor for all $k < \sqrt{n}/4$.
  Our key technical idea is identifying an explicit, deterministic linear operator $\mathsf{x}$ such that a fixed quadratic form of $\mathsf{x}^{2\ell}$ exactly equals the expected trace moments of the SYK Hamiltonian for every $n$ and $k$. This linear operator can be naturally viewed as a \emph{twisted} model of bosons on the space of hyperedges of a hypergraph. The problem thus reduces to identifying the spectral edge of $\mathsf{x}$, which we show is dominated by the spectrum of a natural ${n \choose k}$-dimensional matrix from the \emph{Johnson} scheme and is straightforward to compute using known results.
  To show that our bound is sharp, we construct a witness state with a large quadratic form on $\mathsf{x}$ and transform it into a certificate of a lower bound on the largest quadratic form on $H_{\operatorname{SYK}}$.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously proves that the expected operator norm of the SYK Hamiltonian (with k-body interactions on n Majorana modes) equals (1-o(1))*√(2n)/k for super-constant k ≤ o(√n), confirming previous predictions. The proof introduces a deterministic linear operator 𝘅 whose trace moments match those of the SYK Hamiltonian, reducing the spectral analysis to a Johnson scheme matrix. The bound is sharp via a constructed witness state.
AI.motivation: To rigorously confirm predicted scaling of the SYK Hamiltonian's operator norm and answer open questions in the literature, while also providing provable guarantees for quantum algorithms computing ground state energies.
AI.method: Identifies an explicit deterministic linear operator 𝘅 (a twisted boson model on hypergraph hyperedges) such that quadratic forms of 𝘅^(2ℓ) exactly match the expected trace moments of the SYK Hamiltonian. Reduces the spectral edge problem to the spectrum of a matrix from the Johnson scheme, computable via known results. Sharpness shown by constructing a witness state with large quadratic form on 𝘅, transformed into a lower bound certificate for H_SYK.
AI.result: 𝔼‖H_SYK‖_op = (1 - o(1))·√(2n)/k for super-constant k ≤ o(√n). Extends to sparse SYK. As corollary, the dissipative quantum algorithm of Basso, Chen and Dalzell provably computes the ground state energy up to O(1)-multiplicative factor for all k < √n/4.
AI.conclusion: The expected operator norm scaling is rigorously confirmed, the Johnson scheme connection provides a clean analytical framework, and the results have direct implications for the provable efficiency of quantum algorithms for SYK ground state estimation.

title: Very Strong Irreversibility of Quantum Entanglement
summary: The manipulation of quantum entanglement is fundamentally irreversible: some mixed entangled states require pure entanglement for their preparation, although no pure entanglement can be recovered from them by local operations and classical communication. This irreversibility is known to persist even under the maximal class of operations that do not generate entanglement, revealing a fundamental distinction between entanglement theory and thermodynamics. We construct cases for which any attempt to restore reversibility necessarily incurs an error that increases exponentially with the number of copies. Technically, we demonstrate a strict separation between the exponential strong-converse distillable entanglement and the exponential strong-converse entanglement cost. Our result resolves a conjecture posed by Lami and Regula (Nat. Phys. 19, 184-189 (2023)) and strengthens it by showing that the irreversibility of entanglement persists even at the level of polynomially (in the number of copies) growing error. We further derive a semidefinite-programming lower bound on the exponential strong-converse cost under non-entangling operations. Finally, for the class of completely PPT-preserving operations, we construct analytically solvable families of antisymmetric states exhibiting the exponential strong-converse irreversibility. Remarkably, to our knowledge, no analogous separation between exponential strong converse cost and the analogous distillable entanglement is currently known even under the more restrictive class of LOCC operations.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that entanglement manipulation irreversibility persists even when allowing polynomially growing errors, with an exponential separation between distillable entanglement and entanglement cost, resolving a conjecture by Lami & Regula (2023).
AI.motivation: To understand whether the fundamental irreversibility of entanglement manipulation (analogous to the second law in thermodynamics) can be overcome by allowing errors that grow with the number of copies, and to resolve a conjecture about the persistence of irreversibility.
AI.method: The authors demonstrate a strict separation between exponential strong-converse distillable entanglement and exponential strong-converse entanglement cost using semidefinite-programming lower bounds, and construct analytically solvable families of antisymmetric states under completely PPT-preserving operations.
AI.result: Irreversibility persists even at the level of polynomially growing errors, with an exponential error cost for any attempt to restore reversibility. A strict separation between exponential strong-converse distillable entanglement and cost is established.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement manipulation remains fundamentally irreversible under broad conditions, and no analogous separation is currently known even under LOCC operations, highlighting a deep asymmetry in entanglement theory.

title: Fault-Tolerant Logical Operations and Efficient State Preparation in Modular Quantum Architectures with Noisy Interfaces
summary: Modular quantum computing is a leading paradigm for scaling quantum computation beyond the resource limitations of monolithic devices. In this architecture, multiple quantum processing units (QPUs), employing identical or distinct qubit modalities, are interconnected via shared entanglement. Here, we investigate how errors at module interfaces and within individual QPUs affect fault-tolerant computation when qubits are encoded using the rotated surface code. Going beyond the logical-memory benchmark, we perform circuit-level simulations of fault-tolerant nonlocal CNOT gates implemented via lattice surgery between QPUs connected by noisy Bell pairs, and analyze the resulting logical error rates. Our results show that interfaces can tolerate noise up to an order of magnitude higher than intra-QPU noise, with only a minor reduction in the fault-tolerance threshold. We further develop an efficient protocol for preparing distributed fault-tolerant logical GHZ states, reducing ancilla overhead, time, and nonlocal Bell-pair consumption. We show that ancilla minimization in this setting is equivalent to a vertex-cover problem on an associated graph, and introduce a polynomial-time heuristic algorithm for finding low-overhead solutions. Our results provide quantitative evidence that distributed quantum error correction can enable scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computation in modular architectures.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates fault-tolerant modular quantum computing using rotated surface codes, showing that inter-QPU interfaces can tolerate up to 10x higher noise than intra-QPU components with minimal threshold reduction. It also presents an efficient protocol for preparing distributed logical GHZ states, reducing ancilla overhead by mapping minimization to a vertex-cover problem solved via a polynomial-time heuristic.
AI.motivation: To understand how errors at module interfaces and within individual QPUs affect fault-tolerant computation in modular quantum architectures, which is crucial for scaling beyond monolithic device limitations.
AI.method: Circuit-level simulations of fault-tolerant nonlocal CNOT gates via lattice surgery between QPUs connected by noisy Bell pairs, analyzing logical error rates. Also develops an ancilla-minimization protocol for distributed GHZ state preparation reduced to a vertex-cover problem with a polynomial-time heuristic.
AI.result: Interfaces can tolerate up to an order of magnitude higher noise than intra-QPU noise with only minor reduction in fault-tolerance threshold. The proposed GHZ protocol reduces ancilla overhead, time, and nonlocal Bell-pair consumption.
AI.conclusion: Distributed quantum error correction can enable scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computation in modular architectures.

title: Practical Quantum Topological Data Analysis with Applications to High-Dimensional Feature Extraction and Time Series Analysis
summary:
Topological data analysis (TDA) provides a powerful framework for extracting information about the shape of complex, unstructured data, but the classical cost of computing high dimensional topological features limits its application. Quantum algorithms for TDA offer a route around this bottleneck, yet existing approaches typically focus on exact or high precision Betti number estimation, making the regime for practical quantum advantage appear narrow. Here, we instead frame quantum TDA as a feature-extraction method for downstream data analysis by extracting low-order spectral information from the combinatorial Laplacian as a proxy for high-dimensional topology.
  We support this perspective from both the application and algorithmic sides. First, we show that higher-order TDA features improve predictive performance in two time-series applications: functional MRI analysis for neurodegenerative disease classification and financial time-series analysis for identifying market instability. Second, we develop a moment-based quantum algorithm and show that low-order moments, including the relative trace, are strongly correlated with high-dimensional Betti information, even when the relative Betti number is small. Finally, we present circuit constructions, resource estimates, quantum-classical crossover projections, and experimental results from a Barium development system similar to the forthcoming IonQ Tempo line, extracting Laplacian-derived observables from graph instances and quantitatively comparing them with exact Betti information.
  Together, these results establish quantum TDA as a practical approach for extracting topological features from classically challenging data

AI.tldr: This paper re-frames quantum topological data analysis (TDA) as a feature extraction method for downstream tasks, using low-order spectral information from the combinatorial Laplacian as a proxy for high-dimensional topology. The authors demonstrate practical utility in two applications (fMRI analysis and financial time-series), develop a moment-based quantum algorithm, and provide circuit implementations with resource estimates and experimental results on a quantum system.
AI.motivation: Classical TDA is computationally expensive for high-dimensional features, and existing quantum TDA approaches focus on exact or high-precision Betti number estimation, which limits the regime for practical quantum advantage. The authors aim to establish a more practical framework where quantum TDA serves as a feature extraction method for downstream analysis.
AI.method: The authors propose a moment-based quantum algorithm that extracts low-order spectral information (e.g., relative trace) from the combinatorial Laplacian as a proxy for high-dimensional Betti numbers. They validate the approach on two time-series applications (fMRI for neurodegenerative disease classification and financial data for market instability detection) and provide circuit constructions, resource estimates, crossover projections, and experimental results on a Barium-based quantum system.
AI.result: Higher-order TDA features improve predictive performance in both fMRI and financial time-series applications. Low-order moments, including the relative trace, are strongly correlated with high-dimensional Betti information even when the relative Betti number is small. Experimental results from a Barium development system demonstrate extraction of Laplacian-derived observables that quantitatively compare well with exact Betti information.
AI.conclusion: Quantum TDA can be practically deployed as a feature extraction method for downstream data analysis, using low-order spectral proxies rather than exact Betti numbers. This perspective broadens the potential for quantum advantage in real-world applications.
